# Margaret Brundage

#### Born: December 9, 1900 | Died: April 9, 1976

![Image 3: Margaret Brundage](https://www.illustrationhistory.org/images/made/images/uploads/MargaretBrundage_CoCreateC_580_385_c1.jpg)
## Biography

**Margaret Brundage** (1900-1976) was a key cover artist in the 1930s for the legendary _Weird Tales_ pulp magazine. She studied at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Chicago Academy of Fine Arts in the 1920s before finding employment as an artist for fashion designers. After presenting sample work to the delighted editor of _Weird Tales_ magazine in 1932, Brundage began working full-time for the pulp magazine, though her first cover was for the September 1932 issue of _Oriental Stories_.

Similar in form to the work of the popular pin-up artist **Rolf Armstrong**, Brundage created many of her covers using pastels. As with other female illustrators of the period, she omitted her first name from her signature on the artwork, signing:“M. Brundage.”This led many to believe the artist was male, particularly given the themes of the lurid covers which frequently featured scantily clad female victims. Once it was revealed that the artist behind these shocking covers was a woman, readers became outraged. Given the public outcry and the move of the publisher of _Weird Tales_, Popular Fiction Publishing Company,from Chicago to New York in 1938, Brundage retired from her career as a pulp artist later that year.

Signifying the artist's continued popularity, in 2008 her September 1932 cover art for _Weird Tales_ was sold at auction for over $50,000.

# Margaret Brundage

#### Born: December 9, 1900 | Died: April 9, 1976

![Image 3: Margaret Brundage](https://www.illustrationhistory.org/images/made/images/uploads/MargaretBrundage_CoCreateC_580_385_c1.jpg)
## Biography

**Margaret Brundage** (1900-1976) was a key cover artist in the 1930s for the legendary _Weird Tales_ pulp magazine. She studied at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Chicago Academy of Fine Arts in the 1920s before finding employment as an artist for fashion designers. After presenting sample work to the delighted editor of _Weird Tales_ magazine in 1932, Brundage began working full-time for the pulp magazine, though her first cover was for the September 1932 issue of _Oriental Stories_.

Similar in form to the work of the popular pin-up artist **Rolf Armstrong**, Brundage created many of her covers using pastels. As with other female illustrators of the period, she omitted her first name from her signature on the artwork, signing:“M. Brundage.”This led many to believe the artist was male, particularly given the themes of the lurid covers which frequently featured scantily clad female victims. Once it was revealed that the artist behind these shocking covers was a woman, readers became outraged. Given the public outcry and the move of the publisher of _Weird Tales_, Popular Fiction Publishing Company,from Chicago to New York in 1938, Brundage retired from her career as a pulp artist later that year.

Signifying the artist's continued popularity, in 2008 her September 1932 cover art for _Weird Tales_ was sold at auction for over $50,000.

Joseph Christian (J.C.)Leyendecker (March 23, 1874 – July 25, 1951) was a German-born American illustrator who became one of the most influential figures of the Golden Age of American Illustration.   
  
He produced illustrations, advertisements, posters, and over 400 magazine covers between the late 1890s and 1950, including 322 covers for The Saturday Evening Post.   
More for that publication than any other artist of his time.   
  
Leyendecker created iconic imagery such as the Arrow Collar Man and the New Year’s Baby, helped define visual traditions around American holidays, and shaped the look of early 20th-century advertising. His stylish, dynamic compositions and mastery of figure drawing profoundly influenced later illustrators, most notably Norman Rockwell. J.C. Leyedecker helped establish the modern magazine cover as an art form.  
  
But like most artist today. He is being rediscovered and admired not only for the art he created but the life he lived. He set the bar for artist moving into the 20th century and American artist were forever changed by his achievements in advertisement.

The most famous one is indeed JC Leyendecker, and at the time, he won a scholarship in France, which was back then the epicenter of the occidental fine arts, either at the Beaux Arts or l’Academie Julien.  
The scholarship was made for one person, but JC decided that he would not leave his brother behind that had the same dream and vocation, and split the scholarship with him to bring him to Paris.

# [ART & ARTISTS](https://poulwebb.blogspot.com/)

Named "A Blog of Note" by Google

## Wednesday, 6 January 2021


### Fortune magazine -part 1

Fortune is an American multinational business magazine headquartered in New York City.The publication was founded by Henry Luce in 1929. The magazine competes with Forbes and Bloomberg Businessweek in the national business magazine category and distinguishes itself with long, in-depth feature articles.

The magazine regularly publishes ranked lists, including the Fortune 500,a ranking of companies by revenue that it has published annually since 1955. The magazine is also known for its annual Fortune Investor’s Guide.

At a time when business publications were little more than numbers and statistics printed in black and white,Fortune was an oversized 11”×14" using creamy heavy paper, and art on a cover printed by a special process.Fortune was also noted for its photography, featuring the work of Margaret Bourke-White, Ansel Adams,and others.

During the Great Depression, the magazine developed a reputation for its social conscience. From its launch in 1930 to 1978, Fortune was published monthly. In January 1978, it began publishing biweekly. In October 2009, citing declining advertising revenue and circulation, Fortune began publishing every three weeks. As of 2018, Fortune is published 14 times a year.

Fred Ludekens (1900-1892) was born in Hueneme,California. Although he had no formal training in art, he found work as a billboard painter. Paolo Garretto (1903 Naples - 1989) There was hardly a noteworthy American magazine that had not published Garretto’s work at one time. There were virtually no French, Italian, English, and German poster hoardings or kiosks on which his advertisements did not regularly appear. His airbrushed caricature epitomised Deco styling. During the Twenties and Thirties he was a master of international advertising design and editorial art.

Garretto’s fame in the United States was due to the regularity with which his work appeared in Fortune, Time, Vogue, and The New Yorker, but even more directly owing to his work in the original Vanity Fair.

Alonzo C. Webb (1888 – 1975) was an American etcher, architect, painter and illustrator born in Nashville, Tennessee. From 1907 to 1909, he attended the Art Institute of Chicago. From 1912 to 1913 he studied architecture at the University of Illinois. He later attended the Art Students League of New York and worked with Dan Barber, a New York architect. Around 1920, he started etching and his work began appearing frequently in the French weekly L’Illustration. During the 1920s and 1930s Webb lived and worked in both France and the United States.In the late 1930s he moved to London, where he died in 1975.

Roger Duvoison (1904 - ?) was born in Switzerland into a family with a strong orientation towards the arts. His father was an architect and his godmother was a famous enamel painter. He was recruited into designing textiles which took him to Paris. In 1927, he was recruited by an American textile firm in New York to come and work for them. He made a commitment to relocate for a minimum of four years and he and and his wife moved to New York. He found fame as author and illustrator of numerous children's books.

Antonio Petruccelli (1907 - 1994) was born in Fort Lee, New Jersey. He developed his artistic talent at an early age and began his career as a textile designer. After winning several House Beautiful cover illustration contests, he became a freelance illustrator in 1932; subsequently his work appeared on the covers of Fortune, The New Yorker, Collier’s, Today and House Beautiful magazines. The art director for Fortune, Francis Brennan, said of Petruccelli, “Tony was Mr. Versatility for Fortune. He could do anything, from charts and diagrams to maps, illustrations, covers and caricatures.” Throughout his life, Petruccelli won many important design awards including a U.S. Postage stamp for the American Steel Industry’s 100th anniversary and a Bicentennial medal for the state of New Jersey.

### Fortune magazine -part 1

Fortune is an American multinational business magazine headquartered in New York City.The publication was founded by Henry Luce in 1929. The magazine competes with Forbes and Bloomberg Businessweek in the national business magazine category and distinguishes itself with long, in-depth feature articles.

The magazine regularly publishes ranked lists, including the Fortune 500,a ranking of companies by revenue that it has published annually since 1955. The magazine is also known for its annual Fortune Investor’s Guide.

At a time when business publications were little more than numbers and statistics printed in black and white,Fortune was an oversized 11”×14" using creamy heavy paper, and art on a cover printed by a special process.Fortune was also noted for its photography, featuring the work of Margaret Bourke-White, Ansel Adams,and others.

During the Great Depression, the magazine developed a reputation for its social conscience. From its launch in 1930 to 1978, Fortune was published monthly. In January 1978, it began publishing biweekly. In October 2009, citing declining advertising revenue and circulation, Fortune began publishing every three weeks. As of 2018, Fortune is published 14 times a year.

Winthrop Stark Davis (1885-1950) was born in Boston, Massachusetts. He subsequently lived and worked in Chicago, where he was affiliated with several arts institutions including the Palette and Chisel Club. Davis exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1924 and at the Chicago Galleries Association in 1930, winning prizes in both shows.

During the 1920s and 1930s Stark Davis’s illustrations appeared on covers of the Ladies’ Home Journal, and in numerous advertisements, and from 1927 to 1929, Davis’s artistic and colourful “Bird Series” of advertisements for Lincoln automobiles ran in popular magazines such as Country Life and Home and Garden.

Charles Melville Dewey(1849–1937) was an American tonalist painter.Confined to his bed from his twelfth to his seventeenth year by a hip disease, he formed the poetic conception of nature that appears in his pictures. He studied in the schools of the National Academy of Design, New York, and in Paris under Carolus-Duran,whom he assisted to paint a ceiling in the Louvre. In 1878 he returned to New York. His landscapes in oil and watercolour are in many public galleries and private collections in the United States.

Fred Ludekens (1900-1892) was born in Hueneme,California. Although he had no formal training in art, he found work as a billboard painter. He joined the advertising agency of Lord & Thomas in 1931, and transferred to the company’s New York City office in 1939. He returned to San Francisco in 1945. Ludekens worked in a variety of media, often depicting rural scenes such as fruit ranches, coastal scenes, and the Indians of the Southwest. He produced story, article and cover illustrations for many magazines.

Paolo Garretto (1903 Naples - 1989) There was hardly a noteworthy American magazine that had not published Garretto’s work at one time. There were virtually no French, Italian, English, and German poster hoardings or kiosks on which his advertisements did not regularly appear. His airbrushed caricature epitomised Deco styling. During the Twenties and Thirties he was a master of international advertising design and editorial art.

Garretto’s fame in the United States was due to the regularity with which his work appeared in Fortune, Time, Vogue, and The New Yorker, but even more directly owing to his work in the original Vanity Fair.

Diego Rivera (1886 – 1957) was a prominent Mexican painter born in Guanajuato. He was an active communist, and the husband of painter Frida Kahlo. His large wall works in fresco helped establish the Mexican Mural Renaissance. Between 1922 and 1953, Rivera painted murals among others in Mexico City, Chapingo, Cuernavaca, San Francisco, Detroit, and New York City. In 1931, a retrospective exhibition of his works was held at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Alonzo C. Webb (1888 – 1975) was an American etcher, architect, painter and illustrator born in Nashville, Tennessee. From 1907 to 1909, he attended the Art Institute of Chicago. From 1912 to 1913 he studied architecture at the University of Illinois. He later attended the Art Students League of New York and worked with Dan Barber, a New York architect. Around 1920, he started etching and his work began appearing frequently in the French weekly L’Illustration. During the 1920s and 1930s Webb lived and worked in both France and the United States.In the late 1930s he moved to London, where he died in 1975.

Antonio Petruccelli (1907 - 1994) was born in Fort Lee, New Jersey. He developed his artistic talent at an early age and began his career as a textile designer. After winning several House Beautiful cover illustration contests, he became a freelance illustrator in 1932; subsequently his work appeared on the covers of Fortune, The New Yorker, Collier’s, Today and House Beautiful magazines. The art director for Fortune, Francis Brennan, said of Petruccelli, “Tony was Mr. Versatility for Fortune. He could do anything, from charts and diagrams to maps, illustrations, covers and caricatures.” Throughout his life, Petruccelli won many important design awards including a U.S. Postage stamp for the American Steel Industry’s 100th anniversary and a Bicentennial medal for the state of New Jersey.

## J.C.Leyendecker:America’s Master Illustrator

| Written by | [Saige Jedele](https://www.thehenryford.org/search?&Tab=collections&AuthorIds=321a9e61-00ef-446a-b6f3-209c06139332) |
| --- |
| Published | 2/26/2024 |

One of the most prolific and popular artists of the early 20th century, J.C. Leyendecker created iconic advertising and magazine illustrations that made a lasting impression on American culture.

![Image 11: Advertisement for Arrow Collars, featuring Leyendecker’s iconic Arrow Collar Man, The Saturday Evening Post, July 5, 1924.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/thf704785.jpg?sfvrsn=d5b57f1a_0)  

_Advertisement for Arrow Collars, featuring Leyendecker’s iconic Arrow Collar Man,_ The Saturday Evening Post, _July 5, 1924. / [THF704785](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534968#slide=gs-603593)_

  
**#### Advertising**  

Joseph Christian Leyendecker, known as J.C., was born in 1874 in Germany. He moved with his family in 1882 to Chicago, where he studied art and entered the burgeoning field of commercial illustration. Leyendecker honed his artistic skills in Paris during the 1890s, when advertising posters by artists including Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec and Jules Chéret reached the height of their popularity.

Leyendecker relocated in 1902 to New York City. It was an advantageous time and place for a budding commercial artist, as a growing number of manufacturers sought illustrators for advertisements to help differentiate their consumer goods from the competition. Leyendecker created images that promoted a wide range of products — from Ivory soap and Gillette razors to Karo corn syrup and Kellogg’s cereal — but he made his mark in menswear. For a campaign advertising Cluett Peabody & Co.’s line of Arrow brand shirts, collars and cuffs, Leyendecker produced illustrations of handsome men who exuded style and sophistication. As the [Gibson Girl](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534938#slide=gs-604012) had defined femininity at the end of the previous century, Leyendecker’s popular images, known collectively as the Arrow Collar Man, became a cultural phenomenon that set a new standard for men’s fashion and beauty. Cluett Peabody & Co. reportedly received piles of fan mail addressed to the Arrow Collar Man, who was referenced in popular literature, music and theater. The campaign propelled Leyendecker’s professional career and profoundly impacted his personal life. Charles Beach, an early and frequent model for Leyendecker’s Arrow collar illustrations, became his lifelong partner.

![Image 12: Early 1920s advertisement for Chicago-based clothier B. Kuppenheimer & Co by Leyendecker.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/detail_thf109556.png?sfvrsn=2f0f32c5_0)  

_Leyendecker’s illustrations of fashionable men helped change the advertising landscape, as evidenced by this early 1920s advertisement for Chicago-based clothier B. Kuppenheimer & Co. / Detail, [THF109556](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/182507)_

The Arrow Collar Man reflected a broader shift in marketing, toward bold visuals that connected everyday products with an aspirational lifestyle. Leyendecker excelled in this, employing his trademark depictions of fashionable men in successful campaigns for a wide range of clients. His illustrations sold an idea of glamour and luxury that average consumers could only hope to experience — even if they purchased the shaving cream, suit or [automobile](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534911) being advertised. Leyendecker’s illustrations were widely imitated and helped change the advertising landscape. Americans encountered them everywhere.

![Image 13: Leyendecker’s cover for the June 4, 1904, issue of Collier’s illustrated the first of a series highlighting outdoor sports and leisure.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/thf704891.jpg?sfvrsn=384f5bb5_0)  

_Leyendecker’s cover for the June 4, 1904, issue of_ Collier’s _illustrated the first article in a series highlighting outdoor sports and leisure. / [THF704891](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534962)_

  
**#### Magazines**  

Leyendecker’s talents translated well to the magazine format. He contributed to nearly every major national publication and was soon recognized for his cover illustrations. Leyendecker completed more than 500 magazine covers over the course of his career, including 321 for the popular weekly publication _The Saturday Evening Post_. His imaginative cover designs became favorites among readers, who easily picked them out from competing imagery at busy newsstands.

![Image 14: Leyendecker’s now-iconic depiction of Santa Claus featured on the December 20, 1930, cover of The Saturday Evening Post.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/thf704790.jpg?sfvrsn=f097c92a_0)  

_Leyendecker’s now-iconic depiction of Santa Claus featured on the December 20, 1930, cover of_ The Saturday Evening Post _. / [THF704790](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534978)_

Leyendecker’s early magazine covers illustrated stories printed within each issue, but he was soon given license to create covers around general themes of his choosing. In these images, Leyendecker both captured and helped shape the imagery of American culture — something perhaps best represented by his depictions of holiday traditions. Readers of _The Saturday Evening Post_ looked forward to Leyendecker’s holiday covers year-round, eagerly awaiting his [New Year’s babies](https://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/2014/12/new-years-babies/), with their timely messages about the year to come, and wholeheartedly embracing his jolly, now-iconic Santa Claus.

![Image 15: Leyendecker’s World War I poster, 'Weapons for Liberty,' advertising war bonds, 1917.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/thf62415.jpg?sfvrsn=62f91f19_0)  

_Leyendecker’s World War I poster, “Weapons for Liberty,” advertising war bonds, 1917. / [THF62415](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/45162)_

  
**#### Leyendecker’s Legacy**  

Through his advertising and magazine illustrations, Leyendecker gained renown as an artist who could tell a complete, compelling story through a single image. Recognizing this, the U.S. government called on him to create posters during both world wars, further cementing him as one of America’s best-known illustrators.

Leyendecker appealed to popular audiences and fellow artists alike. One young illustrator, [Norman Rockwell](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/expert-sets/101800/), revered Leyendecker, studied his work and ultimately approached him for advice. Leyendecker, 20 years Rockwell’s senior, became a mentor and friend. His influence is evident in both the younger artist’s style and subject matter. Rockwell would overtake Leyendecker as _The Saturday Evening Post_’s most famous cover artist — and, arguably, become America’s most famous illustrator.

![Image 16: Collier’s illustration, June 4, 1904.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/detail_thf704894.png?sfvrsn=bf402fa0_0)  

_Leyendecker’s depictions of men – a marketing innovation in their own time – continue to inform visual storytelling and appeal to new generations of admirers._ Collier’s _illustration, June 4, 1904. / Detail, [THF704894](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534962#slide=gs-604041)_

During his lifetime, Leyendecker helped revolutionize advertising and influenced a new generation of illustrators. Well after his death in 1951, his work continues to resonate and inspire. Costume designers, video game artists and other visual storytellers, including Star Wars creator George Lucas, count Leyendecker among their influences. New scholarship examines his illustrations’ special appeal to some members of the LGBTQ+ community, who recognize and feel encouraged by their coded queer imagery. Leyendecker’s legacy endures in both the work he inspired and the audiences still touched by his illustrations.

You can explore more of [Leyendecker’s work](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/search-results#advancedSearch=1&tab=artifact-results&s.0.in=creators&s.0.for=Leyendecker,%20J.%20C.%20(Joseph%20Christian),%201874-1951&years=0-0&perPage=25&pageNum=1&sortBy=relevance) in The Henry Ford’s Digital Collections.

## J.C.Leyendecker:America’s Master Illustrator

| Written by | [Saige Jedele](https://www.thehenryford.org/search?&Tab=collections&AuthorIds=321a9e61-00ef-446a-b6f3-209c06139332) |
| --- |
| Published | 2/26/2024 |

One of the most prolific and popular artists of the early 20th century, J.C. Leyendecker created iconic advertising and magazine illustrations that made a lasting impression on American culture.

![Image 11: Advertisement for Arrow Collars, featuring Leyendecker’s iconic Arrow Collar Man, The Saturday Evening Post, July 5, 1924.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/thf704785.jpg?sfvrsn=d5b57f1a_0)  

_Advertisement for Arrow Collars, featuring Leyendecker’s iconic Arrow Collar Man,_ The Saturday Evening Post, _July 5, 1924. / [THF704785](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534968#slide=gs-603593)_

  
**#### Advertising**  

Joseph Christian Leyendecker, known as J.C., was born in 1874 in Germany. He moved with his family in 1882 to Chicago, where he studied art and entered the burgeoning field of commercial illustration. Leyendecker honed his artistic skills in Paris during the 1890s, when advertising posters by artists including Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec and Jules Chéret reached the height of their popularity.

Leyendecker relocated in 1902 to New York City. It was an advantageous time and place for a budding commercial artist, as a growing number of manufacturers sought illustrators for advertisements to help differentiate their consumer goods from the competition. Leyendecker created images that promoted a wide range of products — from Ivory soap and Gillette razors to Karo corn syrup and Kellogg’s cereal — but he made his mark in menswear. For a campaign advertising Cluett Peabody & Co.’s line of Arrow brand shirts, collars and cuffs, Leyendecker produced illustrations of handsome men who exuded style and sophistication. As the [Gibson Girl](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534938#slide=gs-604012) had defined femininity at the end of the previous century, Leyendecker’s popular images, known collectively as the Arrow Collar Man, became a cultural phenomenon that set a new standard for men’s fashion and beauty. Cluett Peabody & Co. reportedly received piles of fan mail addressed to the Arrow Collar Man, who was referenced in popular literature, music and theater. The campaign propelled Leyendecker’s professional career and profoundly impacted his personal life. Charles Beach, an early and frequent model for Leyendecker’s Arrow collar illustrations, became his lifelong partner.

![Image 12: Early 1920s advertisement for Chicago-based clothier B. Kuppenheimer & Co by Leyendecker.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/detail_thf109556.png?sfvrsn=2f0f32c5_0)  

_Leyendecker’s illustrations of fashionable men helped change the advertising landscape, as evidenced by this early 1920s advertisement for Chicago-based clothier B. Kuppenheimer & Co. / Detail, [THF109556](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/182507)_

The Arrow Collar Man reflected a broader shift in marketing, toward bold visuals that connected everyday products with an aspirational lifestyle. Leyendecker excelled in this, employing his trademark depictions of fashionable men in successful campaigns for a wide range of clients. His illustrations sold an idea of glamour and luxury that average consumers could only hope to experience — even if they purchased the shaving cream, suit or [automobile](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534911) being advertised. Leyendecker’s illustrations were widely imitated and helped change the advertising landscape. Americans encountered them everywhere.

![Image 13: Leyendecker’s cover for the June 4, 1904, issue of Collier’s illustrated the first of a series highlighting outdoor sports and leisure.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/thf704891.jpg?sfvrsn=384f5bb5_0)  

_Leyendecker’s cover for the June 4, 1904, issue of_ Collier’s _illustrated the first article in a series highlighting outdoor sports and leisure. / [THF704891](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534962)_

  
**#### Magazines**  

Leyendecker’s talents translated well to the magazine format. He contributed to nearly every major national publication and was soon recognized for his cover illustrations. Leyendecker completed more than 500 magazine covers over the course of his career, including 321 for the popular weekly publication _The Saturday Evening Post_. His imaginative cover designs became favorites among readers, who easily picked them out from competing imagery at busy newsstands.

![Image 14: Leyendecker’s now-iconic depiction of Santa Claus featured on the December 20, 1930, cover of The Saturday Evening Post.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/thf704790.jpg?sfvrsn=f097c92a_0)  

_Leyendecker’s now-iconic depiction of Santa Claus featured on the December 20, 1930, cover of_ The Saturday Evening Post _. / [THF704790](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534978)_

Leyendecker’s early magazine covers illustrated stories printed within each issue, but he was soon given license to create covers around general themes of his choosing. In these images, Leyendecker both captured and helped shape the imagery of American culture — something perhaps best represented by his depictions of holiday traditions. Readers of _The Saturday Evening Post_ looked forward to Leyendecker’s holiday covers year-round, eagerly awaiting his [New Year’s babies](https://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/2014/12/new-years-babies/), with their timely messages about the year to come, and wholeheartedly embracing his jolly, now-iconic Santa Claus.

![Image 15: Leyendecker’s World War I poster, 'Weapons for Liberty,' advertising war bonds, 1917.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/thf62415.jpg?sfvrsn=62f91f19_0)  

_Leyendecker’s World War I poster, “Weapons for Liberty,” advertising war bonds, 1917. / [THF62415](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/45162)_

  
**#### Leyendecker’s Legacy**  

Through his advertising and magazine illustrations, Leyendecker gained renown as an artist who could tell a complete, compelling story through a single image. Recognizing this, the U.S. government called on him to create posters during both world wars, further cementing him as one of America’s best-known illustrators.

Leyendecker appealed to popular audiences and fellow artists alike. One young illustrator, [Norman Rockwell](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/expert-sets/101800/), revered Leyendecker, studied his work and ultimately approached him for advice. Leyendecker, 20 years Rockwell’s senior, became a mentor and friend. His influence is evident in both the younger artist’s style and subject matter. Rockwell would overtake Leyendecker as _The Saturday Evening Post_’s most famous cover artist — and, arguably, become America’s most famous illustrator.

![Image 16: Collier’s illustration, June 4, 1904.](https://www.thehenryford.org/images/thehenryfordlibraries/blog-images/detail_thf704894.png?sfvrsn=bf402fa0_0)  

_Leyendecker’s depictions of men – a marketing innovation in their own time – continue to inform visual storytelling and appeal to new generations of admirers._ Collier’s _illustration, June 4, 1904. / Detail, [THF704894](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/artifact/534962#slide=gs-604041)_

During his lifetime, Leyendecker helped revolutionize advertising and influenced a new generation of illustrators. Well after his death in 1951, his work continues to resonate and inspire. Costume designers, video game artists and other visual storytellers, including Star Wars creator George Lucas, count Leyendecker among their influences. New scholarship examines his illustrations’ special appeal to some members of the LGBTQ+ community, who recognize and feel encouraged by their coded queer imagery. Leyendecker’s legacy endures in both the work he inspired and the audiences still touched by his illustrations.

You can explore more of [Leyendecker’s work](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections-and-research/digital-collections/search-results#advancedSearch=1&tab=artifact-results&s.0.in=creators&s.0.for=Leyendecker,%20J.%20C.%20(Joseph%20Christian),%201874-1951&years=0-0&perPage=25&pageNum=1&sortBy=relevance) in The Henry Ford’s Digital Collections.

  

_Saige Jedele is an associate curator at The Henry Ford._

# A collector’s guide to American illustrators

During the first half of the 20th century — the golden age of American illustration — artists such as Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth and Joseph Leyendecker helped to define an idea of national identity. Illustrated with works offered at Christie’s during Modern New York this April.

*   [Collecting Guides](https://www.christies.com/stories/archive?sc_lang=en&storyTypes=3e902883ad544d4aa20538a0ab2332ac)
*   [Global Art](https://www.christies.com/stories/archive?sc_lang=en&storyCategories=28d5086699374b539ddc9e130b064a4e)
*   [Video](https://www.christies.com/stories/archive?sc_lang=en&storyMedia=e09d5991101e48dba43668c3d429d1f1)

[Open link https://cf-images.us-east-1.prod.boltdns.net/v1/static/6057940598001/ed49f85d-1e1a-4104-98e8-98607dc6c873/bb2edf2d-bed9-4ab2-8595-cb826cd02265/1280x720/match/image.jpg ![Image 1: american illustrator](https://www.christies.com/-/jssmedia/images/features/articles/2026/03/modern-collector-updates/possible-illustration-hero.jpg?h=1640&iar=0&w=2650&rev=1cf13e41782a49119bc28c8f079f0c8a&hash=e480d999341aba95a92848507dde1a76b1a5f930)](https://cf-images.us-east-1.prod.boltdns.net/v1/static/6057940598001/ed49f85d-1e1a-4104-98e8-98607dc6c873/bb2edf2d-bed9-4ab2-8595-cb826cd02265/1280x720/match/image.jpg)

[Douglass Crockwell (1904-1968), _Movie Date_, c. 1942](https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-6578839?ldp_breadcrumb=back). Oil and pencil on gessoed Masonite. 28½ x 24 in (72.4 x 61 cm). Estimate: $40,000-60,000. Offered in [Modern American Art](https://www.christies.com/en/auction/modern-american-art-30986/) on 16 April 2026 at Christie’s in New York

The Golden Age of American illustration began in the early 1900s and culminated roughly 50 years later in the cheerful escapism of [Norman Rockwell](https://www.christies.com/features/15-things-to-know-about-Norman-Rockwell-8714-1.aspx), with many well-loved names — Joseph Christian Leyendecker, [Newell Convers Wyeth](https://www.christies.com/features/The-Wyeth-dynasty-of-American-painters-9860-1.aspx), Joseph Kernan — in between.

These artists rose to prominence through illustrated magazines such as _Scribner’s_, _Harper’s_ and _Collier’s_, creating a warm-hearted narrative of American life through their masterful craftsmanship and visual storytelling.

According to Christie’s [American Art](https://www.christies.com/en/departments/american-art) specialist Quincie Dixon, cheaper printing costs and developments in photomechanical reproduction techniques allowed these magazines to invest in eye-catching imagery. ‘The readership of _The Saturday Evening Post_ grew from 1,600 in 1898 to 1 million in 1903 and 6 million in 1960,’ she adds.

For the artists, the job was deceptively simple — to command attention at the newsstand with a single, compelling image. ‘Norman Rockwell once said that _The Saturday Evening Post_ was the greatest shop window in America,’ says Kestenman.

The illustrators depicted humorous scenes from everyday life, investing them with nuance, comic timing, an instinct for character and a keen sense of social observation. At the same time, these pictures ‘reflected a certain kind of American morality’, notes Kestenman, ‘one that was based on freedom, tolerance, democracy and common decency.’

Today, their work is one of the fastest growing markets in American art, she says, with collectors and curators valuing both the technical skill and creative storytelling of the artists, and the historical importance of their work as a record of social change.

As Kestenman puts it: ‘These artists have become part of our collective memory.’

## Norman Rockwell (1894-1978)

A master at mass communication, Norman Rockwell helped to forge a sense of national identity, becoming America’s foremost illustrator.

Born in New York, the artist had his own studio by the time he was 18, from where he created works for Condé Nast and _Boy’s Life_ magazine. In 1916, he produced his first painting for _The Saturday Evening Post_, going on to illustrate hundreds of covers.

Open image in gallery

![Image 2](https://www.christies.com/img/LotImages/2026/NYR/2026_NYR_24167_0098_000(norman_rockwell_ukulele_serenade102909).jpg?mode=max)

[Norman Rockwell (1894-1978), _Ukulele Serenade_, c. 1925](https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-6578840?ldp_breadcrumb=back). Oil on canvas. 26 x 24 in (66 x 61 cm). Estimate: $300,000-500,000. Offered in [Modern American Art](https://www.christies.com/en/auction/modern-american-art-30986/) on 16 April 2026 at Christie’s in New York

Rockwell’s subjects were average Americans, painted with an affection that captured the public’s imagination, and his illustrations became a familiar presence in the nation’s homes.

## Kurt Ard (b. 1925)

Kurt Ard is globally recognised for his narrative and figurative illustrations and paintings published in popular magazines in the 1950s-1970s including _The Saturday Evening Post_, _Readers Digest_ and the _Family Journal_.

Born in Copenhagen, Denmark, Ard began apprenticing to a Danish painter at a young age. He saw Norman Rockwell, American illustrator and painter, as an inspiration. Hence, he looked to smaller newspapers to begin his career. However, due to World War II, commissions were sparse.

Open image in gallery

![Image 3](https://www.christies.com/img/LotImages/2024/NYR/2024_NYR_21774_0024_000(kurt_ard_in_the_dentists_chair115825).jpg?mode=max)

[Kurt Ard (b. 1925), _In the Dentist's Chair_, c. 1957](https://www.christies.com/lot/lot-6477538?ldp_breadcrumb=back&intObjectID=6477538&from=salessummary&lid=1). Tempera on paperboard. 21¾ x 19½ in (55.2 x 49.5 cm). Sold for $100,800 in [Modern American Art](https://www.christies.com/en/auction/modern-american-art-29919/) on 18 April 2024 at Christie’s in New York

After the war, Ard’s work became a household name. His illustrations and paintings were found in popular magazines throughout Europe and America.

He reached a new artist record for his artwork, _[Cowboy Asleep in Beauty Salon](https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-6420126)_ during the [Modern American Art](https://www.christies.com/en/auction/modern-american-art-29603/) Sale in April 2023 at Christie’s in New York. ## Victor Clyde Forsythe (1885-1962)

# A collector’s guide to American illustrators

During the first half of the 20th century — the golden age of American illustration — artists such as Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth and Joseph Leyendecker helped to define an idea of national identity. Illustrated with works offered at Christie’s during Modern New York this April.

[Douglass Crockwell (1904-1968), _Movie Date_, c. 1942](https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-6578839?ldp_breadcrumb=back). Oil and pencil on gessoed Masonite. 28½ x 24 in (72.4 x 61 cm). Estimate: $40,000-60,000. Offered in [Modern American Art](https://www.christies.com/en/auction/modern-american-art-30986/) on 16 April 2026 at Christie’s in New York

The Golden Age of American illustration began in the early 1900s and culminated roughly 50 years later in the cheerful escapism of [Norman Rockwell](https://www.christies.com/features/15-things-to-know-about-Norman-Rockwell-8714-1.aspx), with many well-loved names — Joseph Christian Leyendecker, [Newell Convers Wyeth](https://www.christies.com/features/The-Wyeth-dynasty-of-American-painters-9860-1.aspx), Joseph Kernan — in between.

These artists rose to prominence through illustrated magazines such as _Scribner’s_, _Harper’s_ and _Collier’s_, creating a warm-hearted narrative of American life through their masterful craftsmanship and visual storytelling.

According to Christie’s [American Art](https://www.christies.com/en/departments/american-art) specialist Quincie Dixon, cheaper printing costs and developments in photomechanical reproduction techniques allowed these magazines to invest in eye-catching imagery. ‘The readership of _The Saturday Evening Post_ grew from 1,600 in 1898 to 1 million in 1903 and 6 million in 1960,’ she adds.

For the artists, the job was deceptively simple — to command attention at the newsstand with a single, compelling image. ‘Norman Rockwell once said that _The Saturday Evening Post_ was the greatest shop window in America,’ says Kestenman.

The illustrators depicted humorous scenes from everyday life, investing them with nuance, comic timing, an instinct for character and a keen sense of social observation. At the same time, these pictures ‘reflected a certain kind of American morality’, notes Kestenman, ‘one that was based on freedom, tolerance, democracy and common decency.’

Today, their work is one of the fastest growing markets in American art, she says, with collectors and curators valuing both the technical skill and creative storytelling of the artists, and the historical importance of their work as a record of social change.

As Kestenman puts it: ‘These artists have become part of our collective memory.’

Born in New York, the artist had his own studio by the time he was 18, from where he created works for Condé Nast and _Boy’s Life_ magazine. In 1916, he produced his first painting for _The Saturday Evening Post_, going on to illustrate hundreds of covers.

## Victor Clyde Forsythe (1885-1962)

The artist and cartoonist Victor Clyde Forsythe worked as an illustrator for the _New York World_. He is perhaps best remembered for his comic everyman Joe Jinks, a balding, henpecked husband with a passion for cars.

Forsythe was a close friend of Norman Rockwell, with whom he shared a studio building in New Rochelle, and it was he who first persuaded the younger artist to submit his work to _The Saturday Evening Post,_ saying, ‘Do what you’re best at. You’re a terrible Gibson, but a pretty good Rockwell.’

In 1920, Forsythe abandoned his career as an illustrator to become a landscape painter, moving back to his native California to paint the bleached, wind-racked expanse of the Southwestern desert.

### George Hughes (1907-1990)

George Hughes was a member of the Arlington artists’ colony, the tight-knit group of Vermont-based illustrators, including Norman Rockwell, who worked on _The Saturday Evening Post_.

Estimate: $70,000-100,000. Offered in [Modern American Art](https://www.christies.com/en/auction/modern-american-art-30986/) on 16 April 2026 at Christie’s in New York

Hughes began his career in the late 1920s, leaving the National Academy of Design in New York to contribute fashion drawings and editorial illustrations to _Vanity Fair_ and _House and Garden_.

## Stevan Dohanos (1907-1994)

Born in Ohio in 1907, Stevan Dohanos was one of America’s most popular illustrators in the 1940s and ’50s. Between 1959 and 1994, he designed more than 40 postage stamps, commemorating such historic moments as the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the statehoods of Alaska and Hawaii. He did also did 123 covers for _The Saturday Evening Post_.

# [My Life 100 Years Ago](https://mylife100yearsago.com/ "My Life 100 Years Ago")

[![Image 1](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/cropped-header-photo-resaved-1-1-2026-1-resized-637-1.png)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/)

![Image 2: Norman Rockwell Literary Digest Thanksgiving cover, 1919](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3658-1-2.jpg?w=313)
# Ten 1919 Illustrators I’m Thankful For

6 Replies

Happy Thanksgiving! Or, as we say in South Africa, “Happy Normal Day When Spouses’ Employers Schedule Evening Work Events!”

So I won’t be celebrating with turkey this year, but I do want to pause to think about some people of 1919 I’m particularly thankful for. Last year, I [thanked](https://myyearin1918.com/2018/11/22/10-1918-people-im-thankful-for/) some of my most admired people from 1918. This year, as the end of the decade rolls around, I’m celebrating the illustrators of the 1910s who made the decade such a visual delight to go back to. You can learn about their lives, or, if you’re too zonked out from overeating, skip the words and feast your eyes on their beautiful art.

1.   **Gordon Conway**

[![Image 3](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3661-1.png?w=172&h=224)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3661-1.png)
Gordon Conway, date unknown (fashionmodeldirectory.com)

Gordon Conway, who despite her name was a woman, was born in Texas in 1894, the daughter of wealthy parents. Encouraged in her artistic aspirations by her globetrotting mother, she began her career with Condé Nast at the age of 20. She also designed costumes for film and the stage in New York and in Europe, where she moved in 1920 with her husband. The marriage didn’t last long, but she stayed in London, living with her mother. Conway’s work ethic was legendary, but ill health forced her into early retirement in 1937. She returned to the United States as World War II approached, moved to a family estate in Virginia, and died in 1956.

Here’s how _Vanity Fair_ described her in a contributors column in August 1919:

_She is one of the more temperamentally inclined of the younger artistic set; she finds it absolutely impossible to get any real stuff into her sketches unless she is sitting in the midst of her pale lavender boudoir, and wearing a green brocaded robe de chambre lined with dull gold and having a single rose on the shoulder. Miss Conway is justly proud of the fact that she draws entirely by ear—never had a lesson in her life._

Here are two of her covers for the magazine,

[![Image 4](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/screenshot-1762.png?w=182&h=246)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/screenshot-1762.png)
January 1918

[![Image 5](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/screenshot-1118-1.png?w=184&h=244)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/screenshot-1118-1.png)
August 1918

here is one that Cond é Nast lists as “artist unknown” but sure looks like her,

[![Image 6](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3704-1.png?w=187&h=238)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3704-1.png)
October 1918

and here is an illustration that _Vanity Fair_ rejected but was later used as a Red Cross poster:

[![Image 7](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3701-1.png?w=186&h=256)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3701-1.png)
sites.utexas.edu

The “new women” Conway portrayed helped shape an era.

Thank you, Gordon!

[![Image 8](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png?w=175&h=42)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png)

1.   **Georges Lepape**

[![Image 9](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3666-1.png?w=129&h=176)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3666-1.png)
Georges Lepape, date unknown (babelio.com)

Georges Lepape, born in 1887 in Paris, was a regular cover artist for _Vogue_. He lived in France, aside from a brief stint at Condé Nast in New York. He died in 1971.

Here are some of his _Vogue_ covers from 1919,

[![Image 10](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3675-1-1.png?w=184&h=249)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3675-1-1.png)
January 15, 1919

[![Image 11](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3628.png?w=187&h=246)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3628.png)
June 15, 1919

[![Image 12](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3676-1.png?w=184&h=242)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3676-1.png)
July 15, 1919

and here’s one from _Vanity Fair_.

[![Image 13](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3663-1.png?w=191&h=256)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3663-1.png)
December 1919

Merci, Georges!

[![Image 14](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png?w=179&h=43)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png)

1.   **John Held Jr.**

[![Image 15](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3670-1.png?w=119&h=178)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3670-1.png)
John Held Jr. (Judge magazine, 1923)

John Held Jr. was born in Salt Lake City in 1889, the son of a British convert to Mormonism. He went to high school with future _New Yorker_ founder Harold Ross, a lifelong friend and associate. Held had just about the best job you could have as a soldier in World War I, supposedly copying hieroglyphics from Mayan ruins in Central America but really drawing maps of the coastline and keeping an eye out for German submarines.*

My family had an anthology of _New Yorker_ cartoons when I was growing up, and Held’s woodcuts used to give me the creeps.** So I was surprised to see that he was the artist behind some of _Vanity Fair’s_ cheeriest covers, like these:

[![Image 16](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3635-3.png?w=178&h=232)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3635-3.png)
October 1919

[![Image 17](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3640-1.png?w=183&h=239)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3640-1.png)
November 1919

[![Image 18](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3641-1.png?w=186&h=241)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3641-1.png)
July 1919

Held would go on to do cover illustrations for F. Scott Fitzgerald.

[![Image 19](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3642-1.png?w=187&h=257)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3642-1.png)

Like a Fitzgerald character, he lived a riotous life, marrying four times, earning a fortune, losing most of it in the 1929 stock market crash, and suffering a nervous breakdown. Fitzgerald notwithstanding, his life did have a second act: he designed the sets for the phenomenally successful 1937 Broadway revue _Helzapoppin_ and served as an artist-in-residence at Harvard. He died in 1958.

Thank you, John!

[![Image 20](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png?w=175&h=42)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png)

1.   **Frank Walts**

Last year, my favorite leftist artist was Hugo Gellert, who did several cover illustrations for _The Liberator._ I couldn’t find a trace of him in 1919, though. Luckily, the progressive press had another talented illustrator, Frank Walts.

Walts was born in Indiana (like a surprisingly large number of people I’ve come across in 1919***) in 1877. His art appeared frequently on the cover of _The Masses,_ which shut down in 1917 amid legal problems and was succeeded by _The Liberator_. He drew the January and February 1918 covers for the NAACP magazine _The Crisis,_

[![Image 21: The Crisis cover, January 1918, drawing of African-American woman and daisies](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/photo-crisis-cover-january-1918-e1517426796543.jpg?w=183&h=259)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/photo-crisis-cover-january-1918-e1517426796543.jpg)
January 1918

[![Image 22](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/dubois-crisis.jpg?w=187&h=265)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/dubois-crisis.jpg)
February 1918

both of which I featured on my blog without paying much attention to Walts because I was new at this and not focused on who drew what.

In 1919, Walts drew the cover illustration for the annual children’s issue of _The Crisis_ in October

[![Image 23](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3617.png?w=185&h=267)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3617.png)

as well as the magazine’s July 1919 issue

[![Image 24](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3642.png?w=187&h=265)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3642.png)

and the December 1919 issue of _The Liberator_, which shines in an otherwise mediocre year of _Liberator_ cover art.

[![Image 25](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3678.png?w=186&h=234)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3678.png)

Walts, who also worked as a civil engineer, would go on to illustrate many more covers for _The Crisis_ and _The Liberator_. He died in 1941.

Thank you, Frank!

[![Image 26](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png?w=175&h=42)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png)

1.   **Helen Dryden**

[![Image 27: Photograph of illustrator Helen Dryden, 1914.](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-1978-1.png?w=132&h=208)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-1978-1.png)
American Club Woman, October 1914

I wrote about Dryden in my post for Women’s History Month, so you can read about her life [there](https://myyearin1918.com/2019/03/29/celebrating-womens-history-month/) and enjoy more of her _Vogue_ covers here:

[![Image 28](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3588.png?w=183&h=247)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3588.png)
March 15, 1919

[![Image 29](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3589.png?w=184&h=255)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3589.png)
July 1, 1919

[![Image 30](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3590.png?w=186&h=243)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3590.png)
June 1, 1919

Thank you, Helen!

[![Image 31](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png?w=175&h=42)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png)

1.   **Coles Phillips.**

[![Image 32](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3664-1.png?w=142&h=179)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3664-1.png)
Coles Phillips (Bain News Service, date unknown)

I first noticed Coles Phillips as the artist behind this haunting hosiery ad:

[![Image 33: 1919 ad for Luxite hosiery. Woman with dress blowing, showing hose, standing with man in wheelchair.](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/screenshot-2053-1.jpg?w=185&h=287)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/screenshot-2053-1.jpg)
Ladies’ Home Journal, April 1919

He was born in Ohio in 1880, moved to New York after a few years at Kenyon college, took night classes in art for a few months, and soon established his own advertising agency, because that’s how life worked in 1919, for some people, anyway. Among his employees was the young Edward Hopper. He joined the staff of _Life_ magazine in 1907 and drew his first “fadeaway girl” cover the next year.

[![Image 34](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3650-1.png?w=187&h=240)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3650-1.png)
May 21, 1908

He repeated this technique on many subsequent covers of _Life_ and other magazines, including _Good Housekeeping_, where he was the sole cover artist from 1912 to 1916.

[![Image 35](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3657-1.png?w=189&h=267)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3657-1.png)
January 1916

[![Image 36](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3680-1.png?w=184&h=265)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3680-1.png)
October 1916

[![Image 37](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3681-1.png?w=188&h=264)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3681-1.png)
December 1916

By 1919, though, he was focusing mostly on advertising, and specifically on women’s legs.****

[![Image 38: Coles Phillips Luxite Hosiery ad, woman in pink dress in front of stained glass window sticking out leg, 1919.](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3650-3.png?w=177&h=263)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3650-3.png)
Ladies’ Home Journal, October 1919

[![Image 39](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3616-1.png?w=177&h=263)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3616-1.png)

He contracted tuberculosis in 1924 and died of a kidney ailment in 1927, at the age of 46.

Thank you, Coles!

[![Image 40](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png?w=175&h=42)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png)

1.   **Eric Rohman**

Remember Selma Lagerlöf, the Nobel Prize-winning Swedish author I [wrote about in September](https://myyearin1918.com/2019/09/24/nobel-prize-laureate-selma-lagerlof/)? In the course of researching her life, I came across some amazing Swedish posters for silent films, some of them made from her books. Digging around, I discovered that most are the work of the incredibly prolific Eric Rohman.

Rohman was born in Sweden in 1891. He became an actor and illustrator in the mid-1910s and opened an art studio in about 1920, where he designed posters for Swedish and foreign films. By his own estimate, he produced 7000 posters over the course of his career. He died in 1949.

Here are some of my favorites:

[![Image 41](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3651.png?w=185&h=280)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3651.png)
Out West, 1918

[![Image 42](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3656.png?w=187&h=292)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3656.png)
Bound in Morocco, 1918

[![Image 43](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3681.png?w=189&h=289)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3681.png)
Komtesse Doddy (Countess Doddy), 1919

[![Image 44](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3657.png?w=191&h=299)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3657.png)
We Can’t Have Everything, 1918

Tack, Eric!

[![Image 45](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png?w=175&h=42)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/screenshot-898-1-1.png)

1.   **George Brandt**

House & Garden is one of those 1919-era magazines that consistently punches above its weight in terms of cover art, but in an unassuming way, so it had never occurred to me to ask who the artists behind my favorite covers were.

One of them, I learned, is Henry George Brandt. (The other is [Harry Richardson](https://myyearin1918.com/2019/08/12/my-perfect-1919-summer-morning/), but there is even less information available about him online than there is about Brandt, so Brandt it is.) Brandt was born in Germany in 1862, immigrated to the United States in 1882, and studied at the Art Institute of Chicago from 1911 to 1916. (Yes, in his fifties!) He was a painter and muralist as well as an illustrator. He died in Chicago in 1946.

Here are some of his House & Garden covers:

[![Image 46](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3684.png?w=195&h=257)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3684.png)
July 1919

[![Image 47](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3685.png?w=196&h=258)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3685.png)
September 1919

December 1919

Thank you, George!

9. **Erté**

[![Image 50: Roman Petrovich Tyrtov (Erté)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/screenshot-1453-1.png?w=149&h=231)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/screenshot-1453-1.png)
Erté, date unknown

Erté is a repeat–he was one of the people I was [thankful for last year](https://myyearin1918.com/2018/11/22/10-1918-people-im-thankful-for/). But you can’t talk about illustration in 1919 without talking about him. He was born in Russia in 1894 (real name Romain de Tirtoff–his father wanted him to be a naval officer and he adopted the pseudonym to avoid embarrassing his family*****). He moved to Paris as a young man and began a career as an illustrator and costume designer; Mata Hari was among his clients. _Harper’s Bazar_ hired him in 1915; he would go on to illustrate over 200 covers for the magazine. He later went into theater, designing sets and costumes for ballets, revues, and films. He died in Paris in 1960.

I wasn’t able to find most of Erté’s 1919 _Harper’s Bazar_ covers–they’re missing from Hathitrust, the most reliable source of online magazines, and few and far between on the internet. Here are two I was able to find:

[![Image 51](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3688.png?w=188&h=262)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3688.png)
March 1919

[![Image 52](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3690.png?w=186&h=261)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3690.png)
May 1919

Спасибо (and merci), Erté!

[![Image 53](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Screenshot-898-1.png?w=179&h=43)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Screenshot-898-1.png)

 10. **Norman Rockwell**

[![Image 54](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3672-1.png?w=136&h=184)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3672-1.png)
Portrait of Norman Rockwell, date unknown

It wouldn’t be Thanksgiving without Norman Rockwell. In 1919, his iconic 1943 Thanksgiving picture [Freedom from Want](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_from_Want_(painting)) was still far in the future, but he did do a Thanksgiving cover for the November 22 issue of _Literary Digest_:

[![Image 55](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3658-1.png?w=186&h=280)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3658-1.png)

Rockwell is one of those people I was surprised to come across in the 1910s because he lived well into my lifetime. (Anthologist Louis Untermeyer and poet Marianne Moore are others.) And he _was_ pretty young then, born in New York in 1894. An early bloomer, he became the art editor of _Boy’s Life_ magazine at the age of 19. His first cover for the _Saturday Evening Post_ appeared in May 1916;

[![Image 56](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3692-1.png?w=191&h=249)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3692-1.png)

322 others were to follow.

[![Image 57](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3694-1.png?w=186&h=236)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3694-1.png)
April 26, 1919

[![Image 58](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3697-1.png?w=193&h=260)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3697-1.png)
March 22, 1919

The humor magazines _Life_ and _Judge_ published some illustrations apparently deemed not wholesome enough for the _Saturday Evening Post,_ like this one

[![Image 59](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3604.png?w=186&h=231)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/screenshot-3604.png)
April 16, 1919

and this one, which I featured as one of the [best magazine covers of February 1918](https://myyearin1918.com/2018/02/28/the-best-and-worst-of-february-1918-magazines-stories-cover-art-and-jokes/) and which has lived on as by far my most repinned [Pinterest pin](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/299982025172574261/).

[![Image 60](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/rockwell-judge-e1519829822915.png?w=190&h=219)](https://mylife100yearsago.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/rockwell-judge-e1519829822915.png)

By the time of his death in 1978, Rockwell was one of America’s most beloved artists.

Thank you, Norman!

And last but definitely not least, thanks to all of you who, over the past two years, have turned a personal project into a community. Happy Thanksgiving, everyone!

(UPDATE 11/30/2019: They had turkey–with cranberry sauce–at the work event. So I had my Thanksgiving dinner after all!)
