### Dutch Information Service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Dutch Information Service")]

By 1937, he was completely devolved from the CPN executive.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980123-52) In the same year, Goulooze was ordered by Dimitrov to disband the current OMS in Amsterdam and create a new OMS, with the infrastructure to support communications with Moscow, including new radio operators, electricians and couriers that were to be recruited from the CPN.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980125-54)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197969-57) It was completely separate from the former German Comintern.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980125-54)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197969-57) Goulooze was provided help by Wenzel, who moved to the Netherlands, in early 1937. Wenzel was an expert radio engineer and they discussed plans for the construction of a radio network in the Netherlands.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979383-58)

As a publisher Goulooze, was able to travel widely without restrictions, that enabled him to meet a wide variety of people, and select particular people for particular jobs.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980123-52) In the same year, he received intelligence training at the [Marx–Engels–Lenin Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marx%E2%80%93Engels%E2%80%93Lenin_Institute "Marx–Engels–Lenin Institute") in Moscow.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) By April 1939, van Proosdy had built a radio transmitter that was based on the [Hartley oscillator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartley_oscillator "Hartley oscillator"). Goulooze knew nothing of how wireless telegraphy worked, so delegated the [ciphering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cipher "Cipher") and radio transmission to his employees.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980127-59)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-61)

In June 1939, Goulooze recruited Adam Nagel, a photographer[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197966-62) and communist member of the CPN to work with Wenzel in Belgium.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197958-63) In the same period Goulooze recruited CPN member Jacobus "Co" Dankaart as his deputy in the information service and became the group's treasurer. Dankaart also worked as a [cutout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutout_(espionage) "Cutout (espionage)") between the radio group and Goulooze.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197958-63)

### Non aggression pact

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Non aggression pact")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Winterink_Group.png/250px-Winterink_Group.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Winterink_Group.png)

The Winterink Group in the Netherlands. It was also known as Group _Hilda_

The [Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact "Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact") signed in August 1939, defined neutrality between the ideological rivals of Germany and the Soviet Union. However, it created considerable ideological difficulties for the CPN and the Comintern. The Comintern pursued no policy other than what the Soviet government planned. It labeled the global conflagration as an imperialist conflict and rejected the pact.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980132%E2%80%93133-64)

With the coming of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the ideology of [Popular Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Front "Popular Front") and [United front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_front "United front") were abandoned by communist parties in Europe, and the politics of proletarian class struggle once again became predominant. The [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party") were no longer called to defend the French homeland when France declared war on Germany, so was declared a proscribed organisation. [[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980133-65)

The French government began to persecute Communists in France, leaving the French Comintern, the KPD and Communist Party is disarray.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980133-65) This resulted in Goulooze's organisation becoming increasingly important to Soviet intelligence as the only organisation in Western Europe that could maintain contact with agents on the ground.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979282-6) In the Netherlands, the leadership of the CPN was expanded to cope with the _supposed_ increased work, in fact it was to attempt to balance opposing ideologies on the board.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980135-66) The leadership of the CPN eventually began to disagree with the leadership of the Comintern, their viewpoint becoming diametrically opposed. While the CPN viewed the war as a fight between opposing ideologies, the Comintern believed it was a true power struggle between nations.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980137-67)

### Soviet intelligence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Soviet intelligence")]

In October 1939, [Anatoly Gurevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Gurevich "Anatoly Gurevich"), a Ukrainian [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Intelligence_Directorate_(GRU) "Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU)") agent who was part of a Soviet espionage group that operated in Germany, and Belgium, visited Goulooze to request help to build his espionage network in Belgium.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) Gurevich asked that a temporary wireless telegraphy link be established for his use, while he established his own wireless telegraphy link in Belgian and this was provided by Goulooze and used, until January 1940.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) In July 1940, Gurevich again visited Goulooze, his second visit, to request the reserve cypher code,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-68) that Goulooze had received from his visit to the Soviet Union, the year before.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2)

## Occupation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Occupation")]

After the [occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_in_World_War_II "Netherlands in World War II") of the Netherlands by the Wehrmacht that began on 10 May 1940, a meeting was held by the CPN on 15 May 1940, where it was realised that many of the members would not survive the war and the party itself would have to operate illegally.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980137-67) The secretariat was reformed with many members put in reserve with Paul De Groot, [Jan Dieters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Dieters?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jan Dieters (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan%20Dieters "nl:Jan Dieters")] and [Lou Jansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Jansen_(verzetsstrijder)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lou Jansen (verzetsstrijder) (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou%20Jansen%20(verzetsstrijder) "nl:Lou Jansen (verzetsstrijder)")] forming the triumvirate that gradually brought the illegal CPN into action. During that month, De Groot planned to run the illegal CPN from Moscow and was in contact with Goulooze to arrange passage by ship, but the plan was abandoned when De Groot and Goulooze visited the Soviet trade representative in Netherlands who rejected the idea. [[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980140-69)

De Groot then expounded the idea of editing and printing an illegal newspaper from [Vichy France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France"). Goulooze explored the idea with French and Belgian communists but the plan was found to be impractical and was abandoned. De Groot instructed Goulooze to contact the Comintern executive in Moscow, to make a request for the secretariat to move to Moscow but on 21 June 1940, Dimitrov rejected the idea, informing De Groot that the group had stay in the Netherlands. Dimitrov forwarded detailed instructions to the secretariat on how to resist the occupation.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980140-69)

The members of the secretariat

[![Image 16: Paul De Groot](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Paul_de_Groot_%28kop%29%2C_Bestanddeelnr_920-1109.jpg/250px-Paul_de_Groot_%28kop%29%2C_Bestanddeelnr_920-1109.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_de_Groot_(kop),_Bestanddeelnr_920-1109.jpg)

Paul De Groot in 1967.

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Lou-jansen-1427492419.jpg/250px-Lou-jansen-1427492419.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lou-jansen-1427492419.jpg)

Lou Jansen in 1943.

During the first months of the occupation, individual leaders of the CPN lacked a cohesive approach to resisting the occupation and took a wait-and-see approach on the political front. Goulooze used to time he was contact with the CPN leadership to call for more political activity.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980141-70) From the very beginning Goulooze was in favour of uncompromising and vigorous resistance to the Germans.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5)

During this period, Goulooze was reporting to the Comintern. [[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980141-70) The reports were created by the CPN party leadership. Due to the limited radio contact, he would first send the reports in an abbreviated form, as well as forwarding each completed report to Moscow by courier.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980141-70) In October 1940, the secretariat complained to Goulooze about a summary letter that Goulooze had written, that was critical of the secretariat, of its wait-and-see approach. In a meeting of the CPN leadership, they decided to replace him after holding a vote that resulted in "no confidence". The secretariat had withdrawn from Amsterdam, leaving the OMS in the city.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980142-71)

Goulooze had stated in the letter than they should have maintained more contact with the OMS in city. The secretariat failed to understand that Goulooze was employed by the Comintern executive directly from Moscow, and had no control over him. De Groot contacted the Comintern executive, who dismissed the idea of replacing him and demanded from that point forward all messages meant for the executive go through Goulooze.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980142-71)

### Collaboration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Collaboration")]

On 24 June 1940, the Dutch government withdrew the CPN publication ban and on 26 June an issue of the "[Volksdagblad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Waarheid "De Waarheid")"[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-73) was written.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980137-67) In an article, [Paul de Groot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Groot "Paul de Groot") opined that German aggression was caused by English imperialism and the Dutch [bourgeoisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeoisie "Bourgeoisie"), stating that the [Dutch people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people") had no "enmity" towards the German people and that the Dutch people had "only an interest in friendship and peace with the German people".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980137-67) The article went on by stating:

"It is in the highest interest of the Dutch population that they neither directly nor indirectly, support the warfare of the Allies, but that they observe a true neutrality towards Germany. Restoring peace and friendship with the German people is the first step that the Dutch people can and must take in the interest of restoring general peace. This also means that the Dutch working people must adopt a correct attitude towards the German occupation of our country"[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980138-74)
Goulooze read the "Volksdagblad" article and was vehemently opposed to its printing. He managed to make contact with a Comintern representative, who contacted the Comintern executive in Moscow. They forbade its printing. However, the article was released. At the time, there was some panic in the CPN at the release of the article and how it would be viewed.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980138-74) It did not prevent the CPN and its organs from being banned by the [Arthur Seyss-Inquart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Seyss-Inquart "Arthur Seyss-Inquart") in July 1940.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEForay201266-75)

### Expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Expansion")]

At the beginning of the occupation, Goulooze had recruited one radio engineer, van Proosdy, whose codename was "Frans".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980143-76) The transmitter was hidden in van Proosdy's house in Orteliusstraat in Amsterdam.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) In 1938, CPN member Jan de Laar was recruited by Goulooze and sent to the Soviet Union for technical training in wireless telegraphy and intelligence techniques. When de Laar returned he became an assistant to van Proosdy.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2)

In April 1940, van Proosdy built a radio transmitter for use by a woman in south Amsterdam and by February 1941, she had been trained to use it.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980145-77) In total, five radio operators were eventually recruited by Goulooze by the end of 1941.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980143-76) To ensure a high level of security, Goulooze separated the encryption/decryption of messages by the cypher clerks from the radio transmission process and used couriers to move messages around, with messages hidden in matchboxes, flashlight batteries or rolled in cigarette cases. It resulted in the radio operator's never knowing what the contents of their message were and the cypher clerks not knowing who transmitted the telegrams.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980146-78) At the same time, the people in his network were employed in legitimate roles designed to disguise their illegal activity, for example as municipal workers.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980146-78)

Goulooze used low-power [shortwave radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortwave_radio "Shortwave radio") transmitters that used the 30-metre band (10.100–10.150 MHz) and that were capable of long-distance traffic.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980147-79) The transmission of telegrams took place at different times. As the war progressed, Goulooze passed on messages from the KPD, the CPN and the Comintern. Information on military activity, e.g. armaments, deployment of units along with industrial activity, e.g. production figures, was increasingly also collected and forwarded.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980147-79)

### Request for help

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Request for help")]

In the summer of 1941, [Eugen Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_Fried "Eugen Fried") contacted Goulooze to request his help to expand his radio network in Brussels.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980149-80) Goulooze sent van Proosdy to Brussels in August 1941. van Proosdy was shown a self-built transmitter by the young person who was hosting it, but it refused to work. A new transmitter was delivered by courier to van Proosdy, three weeks later and he managed to make a connection to Moscow.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980151-81)

### CPN Resolve

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: CPN Resolve")]

As the CPN recovered after being banned, a second meeting of the triumvirate was arranged in July 1940, where they updated and prepared new manifestos. They decided to force a general strike in the large metal companies in November and protest against the persecution of Jews. At the end of November, the CPN published an edition of the _[De Waarheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_Waarheid "De Waarheid")_ (_The Truth_).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980152-7)

Goulooze considered the actions too late and was annoyed that the newspaper did not mention the CPN itself.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980153-82) Goulooze, who was in communication with the comintern, was critical of the strike.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980154-83) The comintern sent instructions to direct the goals of the CPN, i.e. not to see their work as proletarian revolution but as a national liberation struggle. The editorials that later appeared in the future versions of the De Waarheid, made the point in clear language, stating it was not about communism, it was about national liberation and return of democratic freedoms.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980156-84) Despite the friction between Goulooze and the executive, the CPN leadership still used Goulooze to pass messages to the Comintern.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980157-85)

### Red Orchestra

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Red Orchestra")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/95/Organisation_of_the_KPD_in_1942.png/250px-Organisation_of_the_KPD_in_1942.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Organisation_of_the_KPD_in_1942.png)

Organisation of the KPD in 1942, showing the lines of communication and the command hierarchy

Main article: [Red Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Orchestra_(espionage) "Red Orchestra (espionage)")

Much more important for the Soviet Union than the CPN and the triumvirate, was the work undertaken by Goulooze for the KPD.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980157-85) From the outset of the war, Goulooze maintained radio links between the area control centre ("Abschnittsleitung") of the KPD in Amsterdam and the area control centre of the KPD in Paris, the Western European Bureau of the Comintern in Paris and Comintern Executive in Moscow.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980172-86) He also managed the links between the Abschnittsleitung in Amsterdam and illegal groups in Germany. [[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980172-86) In 1939, the French KPD groups fell into disarray as the French government banned the [French communist party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_communist_party "French communist party") and interned many of its members.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980172-86) As a result, radio and courier services were cut. The Comintern used Goulooze to bring these various groups back into contact with each other.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980172-86)

### Knöchel Emigre group

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Knöchel Emigre group")]

At a meeting in Moscow in 1940, it was decided that the various KPD Abschnittsleitung in different capitals in Germany should be dissolved, to enable the formation of a new operational leadership in Germany.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980173-87) The intention was for German KPD organiser, [Wilhelm Knöchel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Kn%C3%B6chel "Wilhelm Knöchel")[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-89) to take change of the KPD in Germany.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980173-87)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2009270-90) Knöchel who was considered an exceptionally effective communist resistance organiser, whose alias was "Alfred".[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGebauer2011496%E2%80%93501-91) He had been living in Amsterdam since 1936 and was the leader of an emigre group of German communists. By 1939, he was living in Moscow and was a full member of the Central Committee of the KPD.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeberHerbstKn%C3%B6chel2008-92)

To bring this plan into operation, the Comintern decided the planning stage would be done in Amsterdam, which resulted in Knöchel returning to Amsterdam. Together with [Willi Gall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willi_Gall "Willi Gall"), Knöchel began publishing communist literature that included various leaflets and bulletins, for example "The Enemy Stands in Your Own Country", for distribution in Berlin.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980173-87) From mid-1940, Knöchel with the assistance of Goulooze began to train the emigre group of communists in the Netherlands to work in Germany as political activists and informers.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197971-88) Goulooze was able to obtain blank identity cards, along with official stamps from a colleague that enabled the KPD members who were hiding, to interact with CPN members in Amsterdam and to travel safely to Germany in some cases under [diplomatic protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_protection "Diplomatic protection"). At the time, Goulooze received instructions from the Comintern and Swedish Communist Party in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm")[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980173%E2%80%9374-93) where the KPD leadership emigrated after they were banned. As the Swedish communists were against setting up a radio transmitter link with Amsterdam, Goulooze organised a courier link by sea and when the sailors visited the sea port of [Delfzijl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delfzijl "Delfzijl"), he would pick up a suitcase full of communist brochures, magazines and other literature. In that manner, the Dutch CPN and KPD members managed to read the latest Russian communist literature. The connection by sea, broke down in late 1941 or early 1942 when many Swiss communists were arrested.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980174%E2%80%9375-94)

The first KPD member to travel to Germany with Goulooze's identity documents was [Alfons Kaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfons_Kaps?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alfons Kaps (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfons%20Kaps "de:Alfons Kaps")] who went as an instructor, in January 1941. The next person to travel was [Willi Seng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willi_Seng "Willi Seng"). Albert Kamradt was the third person. The fourth person was [Alfred Kowalke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kowalke?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alfred Kowalke (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred%20Kowalke "de:Alfred Kowalke")].[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980178-95) On the 9 January 1942, Knöchel met Goulooze for a final meeting before travelling to Germany, taking along blank identity papers, a selection of official stamps and communist literature, travelling as an itinerant silver polisher. [[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980179-96) At the time, Goulooze arranged for everything that was published by the Comintern executive in Moscow, to be couriered to Knöchel in Berlin.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980181-97) When he arrived in Berlin, Knöchel started to produce the [hectographed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectograph "Hectograph") "Der Friedenskämpfer" (“The Fighter for Peace,”) that offered detailed accounts of German atrocities across the [eastern front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Front_(World_War_II) "Eastern Front (World War II)").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2009270-90) The May 1942 special edition of "Der Friedenskämpfer" included detailed knowledge of the execution of French, Czechs, Germans, and Norwegians across Europe and as well as specific military companies that carried out executions of Soviet POWs in Leningrad, and civilians in [Lviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv "Lviv"). Knöchel exchanged documents in the form of micro-photocopies with [Elisabeth Schumacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Schumacher "Elisabeth Schumacher").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson200971-98) and [Wilhelm Guddorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Guddorf "Wilhelm Guddorf") who were the intermediaries of [John Sieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Sieg "John Sieg"). It is not known if Sieg ever met Knöchel.

When Knöchel left for Germany, at least 10 communist instructors still had to be recruited and sent to Germany.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99) Arranging the travelling for the instructors became increasingly difficult, due to heavy bombing and increased German security, leaving only a river connection. The difficulty was the lines of radio communication between from the KPD in Germany, to Goulooze DIS and onwards to the Comintern in Moscow.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99) At the time, Knöchel was using two couriers, his common-law wife [Cilly Hansmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Hansmann?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cecilia Hansmann (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A4cilie%20Hansmann "de:Cäcilie Hansmann")], and [Charlotte Garske](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Garske "Charlotte Garske") to move intelligence between Berlin and Amsterdam for transmission to the Comintern. In the late summer 1942, the Comintern and the KPD leadership through [Wilhelm Pieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Pieck "Wilhelm Pieck") began to urge Goulooze to establish a radio communication link in Berlin. Considered an extremely perilous and difficult task, Goulooze selected van Proosdy for this. [[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99)

Van Proosdy had to establish a legal existence in Germany by registering with the _[Arbeitseinsatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbeitseinsatz "Arbeitseinsatz")_. Once that was completed, it was arranged for a letter to be sent by Willem Visser, an employee of a small Berlin based electricity company that was part of [AEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEG_(German_company) "AEG (German company)"), to offer a position of employment to Van Proosdy, as an electrician. [[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99) Van Proosdy left on 2 December 1942, using documentation arranged by Goulooze. In Berlin, he made contact with Knöchel, who introduced him to Kowalke who was to be trained as a radio operator.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99) Goulooze arranged for a radio transmitter to be sent by ship but it never arrived. He then forwarded a small reserve transmitter by ship as a replacement.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980183-100)

### Soviet Parachutists

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Soviet Parachutists")]

[![Image 19](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/KRUYT%2C_John_William.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KRUYT,_John_William.jpg)

Jan Wilhelm Kruyt, who was arrested after parachuting from a plane and breaking his leg

These were agents that were part of [Operation Pickaxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Pickaxe?action=edit&redlink=1 "Operation Pickaxe (page does not exist)")[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTETyas2017106-101) and dropped by aircraft sent from [RAF Tempsford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Tempsford "RAF Tempsford"). accommodated.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980169-102) On 22 June 1942, Jan Wilhelm Kruyt Jr, was parachuted into the Netherlands with a wireless telegraphy set for Goulooze and false papers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) On 24 June 1942, [Jan Wilhelm Kruyt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Kruyt "Willy Kruyt") Sr, an ardent communist and ex-clergyman was dropped by parachute from a British plane in Belgium.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980170-103) Kruyt Sr broke his leg when he landed and was arrested shortly after by the [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo "Gestapo") and sent to [Fort Breendonk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Breendonk "Fort Kousnetzov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kousnetzov?action=edit&redlink=1 "Peter Kousnetzov (page does not exist)") using the alias Bruno Kühn was parachuted into the Netherlands.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980171-105) Kousnetzov was found by Goulooze's men after wandering about the woods for a night.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980171-105) Kousnetzov was originally sent to provide support the Knöchel network in Germany.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197971-88) However, Goulooze was unable to contact Knöchel at the time, so decided to contact the Comintern executive to request that Kousnetzov work with CPN radio operator Jan de Laar instead, which was agreed. ## Sonderkommando Rote Kapelle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Sonderkommando Rote Kapelle")]

On 18 or 19 August 1942 (sources vary), Winterink was arrested[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979389-106)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStadsarchief_AmsterdamInventory_of_the_archives_of_Riek_Milikowski-de_Raat-107) by the [Sonderkommando Rote Kapelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonderkommando_Rote_Kapelle "Sonderkommando Rote Kapelle") at a cafe in Amsterdam, after being betrayed by [Konstantin Jeffremov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstantin_Jeffremov "Konstantin Jeffremov").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStadsarchief_AmsterdamInventory_of_the_archives_of_Riek_Milikowski-de_Raat-107)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979389-106) Nine members of the group with two remaining radios were not discovered and continued to work. A total of 17 people from Winterink's group were arrested. This arrests led to an unpleasant aftermath for Goulooze as rumours were spread by the CPN that it was Goulooze's fault.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980169-102) Winterink's friends even went as far in stating that Goulooze was a member of the [Sicherheitsdienst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicherheitsdienst "Sicherheitsdienst").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980169-102) Due to the rumours, distrust in Goulooze grew to an extent that it was decided by two members of the CPN, Ab Arendse and Piet Groeneveld to kill Goulooze. When their preparations were complete, they contacted Jan Postma, who decided to intervene to prevent the execution.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980169-102)

### Search for Goulooze

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Search for Goulooze")]

On 12 January 1943, Alfons Kaps was arrested by the Sonderkommando [[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980185-108) in [Düsseldorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCsseldorf "Düsseldorf"), following a denunciation.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGebauer2011237-109) Under enhanced torture, he agreed to work for the Sonderkommando as a [double agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_agent "Double agent") or V-Mann,[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-111) first betraying Willi Seng, who was arrested on 20 January 1943 and who was also subject to enhanced torture.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeberHerbst2008-112) After the indictment, Kaps took his own life in March 1943.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980185-108) Through Seng, Knöchel was betrayed and was arrested on 30 January 1943.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980186-113) After he was tortured, Knöchel agreed to become a V-Mann and held a number of meetings with van Proosdy in the normal course of operation, making him effectively under the control of the Gestapo. Van Proosdy eventually realised that Knöchel was a V-Mann, due to his general demeanor and errant behaviour. He decided to make arrangements to return to Amsterdam but was arrested on 22 May 1943 before he could leave. Upon learning from a contact that van Proosdy was arrested and that the Sonderkommando was searching for him, Goulooze went into hiding.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980187-114)

The Sonderkommando first attempted to use van Proosdy's wife in a trick to expose him, but this was unsuccessful. Even when the Gestapo managed to find a photograph of Goulooze, they were unable to locate him.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980187%E2%80%93188-115) By 10 June 1943, Goulooze had informed all his radio and cipher people that it was likely van Proosdy was arrested and that they should go into hiding.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) At the time, all the work and residual addresses were abandoned.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980187%E2%80%93189-116) On the night of 1–2 July 1943, the Gestapo raided all the addresses they had been monitoring and suspected, but it yielded nothing of importance. However, on 2 July, the Gestapo arrested one of Goulooze's radio operators. [[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980190-117) The man was tortured and revealed that he was to meet Goulooze's deputy, Jacobus Dankaart, the next afternoon. However the Gestapo bungled the meeting and the Dankaart was shot twice in the back when he tried to flee.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980191-118) By the end of July several more of the radio people had been arrested and two of the radio sets had been captured by the Sonderkommando. Goulooze informed the Comintern in Moscow through the last transmitter of the situation, that the OMS group would be disbanded.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980192-119) On the 24 August 1943, Dankaart was taken to the Zuidwal hospital in The Hague.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980195-120) This enabled Goulooze to contact Dankaart to arrange an escape plan, which was successful on 18 September 1943.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980196-121) During the following days, the Gestapo operation continued. Comintern agent [Eugen Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_Fried "Eugen Fried") (Clément), Goulooze's collaborator and liaison with the French Communist Party was shot dead in Brussels on 17 August 1943.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980197-122) On the 5 November 1943, Kowalke was executed. During his many months of interrogation, he never exposed any names, which saved the lives of many people in Goulooze's organisation. [[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980198-123) Another close collaborator of Goulooze was [Erich Gentsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Gentsch?action=edit&redlink=1 "Erich Gentsch (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich%20Gentsch "de:Erich Gentsch")] who was the director of the KPD in Amsterdam since 1936. He was arrested in April 1943 and never exposed any names during his interrogation over many months.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980199-124) He was hanged in August 1944.

### Dissolution of the Comintern

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Dissolution of the Comintern")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/928.Joseph_E._Davies_1939.jpg/250px-928.Joseph_E._Davies_1939.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:928.Joseph_E._Davies_1939.jpg)

The American diplomat [Joseph E. Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_E._Davies "Joseph E. Davies") who did so much to disguise the true nature of Stalinist Russia

On the 15 May 1943, Goulooze was listening to the radio broadcasts from Moscow, when he heard that the Comintern had been dissolved on the order of Stalin.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980201-125) For Goulooze, who was a revolutionary, the vision that the Comintern presented was one of a need for world revolution. Harmsen posits that Goulooze must have been disappointed and even expressed some doubt about the value of the work that he had done for the organisation up to that point[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980203-126) but ultimately his revolutionary zeal wouldn't have been extinguished.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980203-126) Goulooze wouldn't have known about the [Stalinist purges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge") that started in August 1936. He came to know about the [trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_of_the_Anti-Soviet_%22Bloc_of_Rightists_and_Trotskyites%22 "Case of the Anti-Soviet \"Bloc of Rightists and Trotskyites\"") of the group associated with [Leon Trotsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Trotsky "Leon Trotsky") after several Comintern officials whom he had met when he visited the Soviet Union and spoke to on the radio were replaced and this swayed his ideology to such an extent that he had a real fear of [Trotskyism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trotskyism "Trotskyism"). He came to know about it through a copy of the memoir by the American diplomat [Joseph E. Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_E._Davies "Joseph E. Davies") "Mission to Moscow", that was passed hand to hand in the Netherlands[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980204-127) that viewed the Soviet [show trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_trials "Moscow trials") under [rose tinted glasses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosy_retrospection "Rosy retrospection"). He never came to realise the true nature of Stalinist Russia. After the war, in 1946, Goulooze published "The great conspiracy; the secret war against soviet Russia" by Michael Sayers and Albert Kahn. The book falsely claims that Trotsky committed treason. Even then Goulooze had no ideological doubts and continued to fight against "fascism".[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980204-127)

After the dissolution of the Comintern, he continued to operate as much as normal as possible, even as the number of arrests increased and the membership of the party dropped from 1200 down to 400.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980205-128) With his liaison work with the Comintern finished, Goulooze turned back to the party, which at the time had broken into disorganised groups.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980211-129) Goulooze contacted Moscow, who advised him to reform the CPN using trusted members from before the war. Goulooze approached Jan Postma who took over the management of the CPN. Postma contacted [Kees Schalker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kees_Schalker "Kees Schalker") and [Ko Beuzemaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko_Beuzemaker?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ko Beuzemaker (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko%20Beuzemaker "nl:Ko Beuzemaker")] and asked Goulooze to help run what remained of the party.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980211-129) One of the first tasks for Goulooze was to arrange a liaison between the CPN and the [Council of Resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Resistance?action=edit&redlink=1 "Council of Resistance (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raad%20van%20Verzet "nl:Raad van Verzet")] that was formed in May 1943.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980212-130) In the following months, Goulooze continued to make contributions to the communist newspapers that were published by the CPN leadership, where they envisioned a unity of socialist and communists and a united trade union movement.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980212-130)

### Arrest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Arrest")]

On 23 October 1943, Goulooze, Postma, [Kees Schalker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kees_Schalker "Kees Schalker") and [Ko Beuzemaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko_Beuzemaker?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ko Beuzemaker (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko%20Beuzemaker "nl:Ko Beuzemaker")] met in an insurance building at [Catharijnesingel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catharijnesingel "Catharijnesingel") in [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht "Utrecht"), with the expectation that the war was coming to an end, with a plan to formulate their positions after the war.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980214-131) A second meeting was arranged in Utrecht for 11 November to continue the post-war planning.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980217-132) However, on 10 November 1943, both Ko Beuzemaker and his wife were arrested, leading to the exposure of the group.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalesloot1986-133) Goulooze, Postma, Cornelis Schalke were subsequently arrested by the [Sicherheitsdienst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicherheitsdienst "Sicherheitsdienst") in Utrecht.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980217-132)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979281-1)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-135)

They were taken to [Herzogenbusch concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herzogenbusch_concentration_camp "Herzogenbusch concentration camp").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) Dankaart had been waiting for a rendezvous with Goulooze who didn't arrive.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980217-132) When he found that the group had been was arrested, he organised a rescue party where 6 men put on the uniform of the [Ordnungspolizei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnungspolizei "Ordnungspolizei"). Some would act as guards and some prisoners and drive to the prison to escort Goulooze out the place. However a patrolling German guard asked them for the daily password, which they didn't know and they were discovered and arrested.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980218-134) Dankaart later managed to escape. Beuzemaker and Schalker, who were barely involved in clandestine activities were executed on 13 January 1944 on the [Waalsdorpervlakte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waalsdorpervlakte "Waalsdorpervlakte").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980218-134)

### Interrogation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Interrogation")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Prisoners_in_the_concentration_camp_at_Sachsenhausen%2C_Germany%2C_12-19-1938_-_NARA_-_540175_%28cleanup%29.jpg/250px-Prisoners_in_the_concentration_camp_at_Sachsenhausen%2C_Germany%2C_12-19-1938_-_NARA_-_540175_%28cleanup%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prisoners_in_the_concentration_camp_at_Sachsenhausen,_Germany,_12-19-1938_-_NARA_-_540175_(cleanup).jpg)

Prisoners in the concentration camp at Sachsenhausen, Germany, 19 December 1938.

Postma was subjected to torture but never exposed any of his collaborators.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980218-134) Goulooze was also tortured and refused to reveal anyone or disclose the locations of the safehouses or radios.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980222-136) In February 1944, he was released from detention and transferred to a seminary in [Haren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haren,_Groningen "Haren, Groningen") where further interrogation began on 21 March 1944 concerning his Belgian contacts. He was taken to Brussels twice for identification, but his stamina, self-confidence and composure enabled him to withstand the torture.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980223-137) At the time, the trial of the other 11 arrestees was held up due to the length of Goulooze's interrogation.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980224-138) There was agreement reached on 11 August 1944 between the Judge and the Sicherheitsdienst that the trial should go ahead without Goulooze.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980224-138) However, by [5 September 1944](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolle_Dinsdag "Dolle Dinsdag"), the liberation of the Netherlands was only hours away, so Goulooze was never tried, instead he was sent to [Sachsenhausen concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sachsenhausen_concentration_camp "Sachsenhausen concentration camp") along with 3000 other prisoners from Haren.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980224-138)

Dutch communist and resistance fighter (1901–1965)

| Organization(s) | [Comintern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_International "Communist International"), [Red Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Orchestra_(espionage) "Red Orchestra (espionage)") |

**Daniël "Daan" Goulooze** (28 April 1901 – 10 September 1965) was a Dutch Jewish construction worker who was a committed communist and resistance fighter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979281-1) In 1925, he became a member of the [Communist Party of the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_the_Netherlands "Communist Party of the Netherlands") (CPN) and by 1930 had become an executive member of the organisation. In 1934, he formed _Pegasus_, a publisher of many left-wing writers and intellectuals in the Netherlands, some for the first time. In 1935–1936, Goulooze formed the Dutch Information Service (DIS), an organisation that supplied information to the Soviet Union.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) Goulooze became the liaison between the organisation and the CPN.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) In 1937, he went to the Soviet Union, where he received intelligence training at the [Marx–Engels–Lenin Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marx%E2%80%93Engels%E2%80%93Lenin_Institute "Marx–Engels–Lenin Institute") in Moscow.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) Upon returning, he became the liaison officer of [Communist International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_International "Communist International") (Comintern) in the Netherlands, his main duty being to maintain on-going radio contact with Soviet intelligence.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBayerleinAlbert201311%E2%80%9313-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEForay201262-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5)

Goulooze used the DIS organisation from early 1937 to help establish Soviet [Red Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Orchestra_(espionage) "Red Orchestra (espionage)") agents in the Netherlands, France and the Low Countries. After the start of the war and the [occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_in_World_War_II "Netherlands in World War II") of the Netherlands, Goulooze helped to reestablish the KPD in Germany in 1940. As the war progressed, the Comintern, the [Communist Party of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Germany "Communist Party of Germany") (KPD) and the [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party") were progressively destroyed in Europe, the DIS became increasingly important to Soviet intelligence as the only organisation in Western Europe that could maintain contact with Soviet agents on the ground.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979282-6)

Such was the level of communication that Goulooze conducted with Soviet intelligence, that he maintained four separate and active [wireless telegraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_telegraphy "Wireless telegraphy") sets and one in reserve.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979281-1) His signals were eventually detected by the German [Funkabwehr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funkabwehr "Funkabwehr") and he was arrested along with many members of the DIS. Goulooze was sent to [Sachsenhausen concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sachsenhausen_concentration_camp "Sachsenhausen concentration camp") but managed to survive the war. In 1948, he was expelled from the CPN[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBayerleinAlbert201311%E2%80%9313-3) after a smear campaign about his role in the war that lasted more than a decade. He then worked for the "De Republiek der Letteren" (The Republic of Arts), a left-wing publishing house. In 1951 he had a heart attack. He died in 1965.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5)

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Nationaal_Arbeids-Secretariaat_Logo.svg/250px-Nationaal_Arbeids-Secretariaat_Logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nationaal_Arbeids-Secretariaat_Logo.svg)

Logo of the National Labor Secretariat

Goulooze was the son of Daniël Goulooze, a [blacksmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blacksmith "Blacksmith"), and Baukje Goulooze (née Visser), a housemaid, and was the oldest of six children, who grew up in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") in a working-class family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) His grandparents on his father's side came from [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeland "Zeeland") in the south, and on his mother's side from [Friesland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friesland "Friesland"), in the northern part of the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) His father was a member of the National Federation of Metal Workers union that was affiliated with the [National Labor Secretariat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Labor_Secretariat "National Labor Secretariat") (NAS, Nationaal Arbeids-Secretariaat) trade union federation. He was an admirer of the Dutch politician and later social anarchist [Ferdinand Domela Nieuwenhuis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Domela_Nieuwenhuis "Ferdinand Domela Nieuwenhuis").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) After the [German invasion of the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_invasion_of_the_Netherlands "German invasion of the Netherlands") in May 1940, his father was interred at the [Herzogenbusch concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herzogenbusch_concentration_camp "Herzogenbusch concentration camp") and died, aged 70, in 1943.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5)

In March 1929, Goulooze entered into a common-law marriage with Lydia Wolters.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) In October 1938, Goulooze and Wolters split. Goulooze entered into his common-law marriage, this time to Petronella Alida van de Plaats (1911-1949), who suffered from poor health. The couple had a son, Zane, born in 1939, to whom the couple were devoted. To protect them, Goulooze moved them to [Gooi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gooi "Gooi") at the start of the war.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980152-7)

## Anarchism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Anarchism")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Gustaaf_Oosterhuis%2C_Afb_010179000215.jpg/250px-Gustaaf_Oosterhuis%2C_Afb_010179000215.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gustaaf_Oosterhuis,_Afb_010179000215.jpg)

A view of the Nederlandsche Scheepsbouw Maatschappij ship yard in 1916, where Goulooze worked at

After leaving school, Goulooze was apprenticed to a carpenter and attended an evening school to supplement his knowledge of carpentry. Politically, as a youth, Goulooze was leftist and this was visible by his youth membership of the [National Labor Secretariat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Labor_Secretariat "National Labor Secretariat") (NLR, Nationaal Arbeids-Secretariaat). He subsequently worked in the drawing school of the Dutch shipbuilding company, [Nederlandsche Scheepsbouw Maatschappij](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nederlandsche_Scheepsbouw_Maatschappij "Nederlandsche Scheepsbouw Maatschappij") in construction.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5)

In 1916, Goulooze joined the Social-Anarchist Youth Organisation (SAJO, Sociaal-Anarchistische Jeugd Organisatie).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDe_Groot196544-8) his was an organisation that was established in several cities including Amsterdam, that consisted of several dozen young rebellious people who refused to do their military service, instead, spending their time going on rambles, and making music as well as planning bombings.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198023-9)

In 1919, Goulooze was elected treasurer.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) In September 1920, Goulooze took over administration for publishing the organisations magazine, _De Opstandeling_ (The Insurgent).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198026-10) Around this time, Goulooze became part of a group of young men and women,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198030%E2%80%9333-11) that formed around Dutch communist and chemigrapher [Jan Postma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Postma?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jan Postma (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan%20Postma%20(CPN) "nl:Jan Postma (CPN)")].[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988b-12)

Postma would go camping with the group, and they would hold discussions and debate politics, communism, [trade unionionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_union "Trade union") and the [Russian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Revolution "Russian Revolution"). Postma strongly supported trade unionism, the soviet revolution, dictatorship for the proletariat and the group initially shared his enthusiasm, but some eventually rejected his views. Goulooze for the most part, found himself in agreement with Postma and this, in turn, developed into a lifelong friendship. The heated debates eventually led to a group withdrawing from the SAJO that included Goulooze, leaving to join the _Federation of Social Anarchists_ of which Postma was a member. On 22 July 1922, Goulooze became the administrator for the _Social Anarchists_ magazine, _De Toekomst_. [[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198030%E2%80%9334-13)

## Nomad

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Nomad")]

The first real decision he made was whether to accept military service during [conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_the_Netherlands "Conscription in the Netherlands") or refuse it.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198050-14) As an anarchist, Goulooze was anti-militaristic and while it was accepted for members of his peer group to refuse the service and wait to be arrested by the [Military police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_police "Military police"), he decided to ignore the conscription order and evade arrest. Goulooze became a nomad, living on his wits, constantly on his guard. During this period, he worked in [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"), among other places. For several years he managed to avoid being arrested. In 1929, when he moved into his own apartment with his wife, he refused to be added to the [Electoral roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_roll "Electoral roll").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198050-14)

However, it became expedient in the early 1930s[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) for Goulooze to rebuild his legal existence and he was finally arrested. However, when he was undergoing his medical examination for conscription, he was rejected due to a minor foot disorder, making the whole exercise moot.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198050-14)

Living a nomadic life did not prevent Goulooze from taking part in a number of political actions in the 1920s and early 1930s. In 1923, Goulooze was responsible for the transportation and distribution of the special newspaper _[De Spelbreker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_Spelbreker?action=edit&redlink=1 "De Spelbreker (page does not exist)")_, not only in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"), but in the rest of the country.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198051-15)

The _De Spelbreker_ newspaper was created by the _Committee of Action_, a group of the Dutch labour movement, made up of Communists, [Syndicalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syndicalism "Syndicalism") and Anarchists, who wanted to protest the 1923 Fleet Act and the 25th anniversary of Queen [Wilhelmina of the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelmina_of_the_Netherlands "Wilhelmina of the Netherlands"). During this period, Goulooze was also working for the NAS. His name appeared in _De Arbeid_, the legal body of trade union on 17 November 1923.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198051-15)

In the same year, the NAS split into two groups. On one side were 8,000 members who left to found the IWA-affiliated [Dutch Syndicalist Trade Union Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Syndicalist_Trade_Union_Federation "Dutch Syndicalist Trade Union Federation") (NSV, [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language"): _Nederlands Syndicalistisch Vakverbond_) that was chaired by [Bernard Lansink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lansink?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bernard Lansink (page does not exist)"). On the other was a group who wanted to join the [Red International of Labour Unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_International_of_Labour_Unions "Red International of Labour Unions") (RILU), although many in the federation favoured the anarcho-syndicalist [International Workers' Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWA%E2%80%93AIT "IWA–AIT") (IWA). Goulooze sided with the NSV and became the organiser of a youth recruitment office at a Local Labour Secretariat (PAS, Plaatselijke Arbeids Secretariaten) in Amsterdam.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198053-16)

## Communist Party of Netherlands

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Communist Party of Netherlands")]

In June 1924, the Federation of Social Anarchists group came to an end.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198051-15) At the time, Goulooze rejected anarchism, along with the Postma group. He became fully Communist, as it was the only political alternative that suited his worldview. Goulooze believed that the anarchists were incapable of an effective struggle against capitalism.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198055-17) Unwilling to join the CPN, he, along with Postma, instead joined the [BKSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Communist_Struggle_&_Propaganda_Clubs "League of Communist Struggle & Propaganda Clubs") on 24 January 1925. Postma went on to become editor of _De Kommunist_, the magazine of the BKSP. [[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198056-18)

Six months later, the BKSP party leadership split, [David Wijnkoop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wijnkoop "David Wijnkoop") along with most of the leadership was forced to resign and a large sector of BKSP opted to rejoin the [Communist Party of Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_the_Netherlands "Communist Party of the Netherlands") ("Communistisch Party Holland") (CPH).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988b-12) By 1925, Goulooze had become an active [communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism "Communism") and in 1926, became a member of the CPH.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVoerman2001398-19) Due to his age, Goulooze became an active member of the [Young Communist League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Youth_Movement_(Netherlands) "Communist Youth Movement (Netherlands)") (CJB, '_Communistische Jongeren Beweging_). Goulooze became a popular and later important member of the CJB. Under Goulooze and in agreement with the political line take by the [Young Communist International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Communist_International "Young Communist International") (KJI, _Kommunist Jeugd Internationale_) the CJB decided to take direct action, instead of the usual discussion of politics.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198058-20)

Under orders from Moscow, it was rearranged into business divisions and the magazine _De Jonge Communist_ (The Young Communist) was renamed to _De Jonge Arbeider_ (The Young Worker).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198058-20) As the CJB was a small organisation, Goulooze tried to create a leadership role that resulted in him negotiating with several companies during spontaneous youth strikes. At the same time, a plan grew to send a delegation to the Soviet Union.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198061-21) Seven young people were delegated from suitable companies and the delegation left at the end of August 1926. When the group returned, a detailed brochure, _What did 7 young workers in Soviet Russia see?_, was published that described their impressions. This was the first of many trips to the Soviet Union he would take.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198061-21)

### A new academy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: A new academy")]

When he returned, Goulooze established a new academy that offered a three-week course to train a cadre of CJB communists. The leaders of the academy were made up of [Henriette Roland Holst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henriette_Roland_Holst "Henriette Roland Holst"), [Gerrit Mannoury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerrit_Mannoury "Gerrit Mannoury"), and [Henk Sneevliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henk_Sneevliet "Henk Sneevliet") and its initial enrollment consisted of sixteen students, aged sixteen to twenty-five.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198061-21) When the academy came to public notice, Goulooze defended it existence, but also took an active part in running the different CJB departments that included canvassing, leafletting, pasting up posters and demonstrating.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198063-22)

In June 1928 in Amsterdam at the CPH party congress, the congress erupted in open warfare. Goulooze was immediately elected as secretary of the board, where he represented the CJB.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVoerman2001370-23) On 17 August 1928, Goulooze attended the [World Youth Peace Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Youth_Peace_Congress?action=edit&redlink=1 "World Youth Peace Congress (page does not exist)") as a representative of the CJB, that was hosted in [Eerde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eerde "Eerde").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198069-24)

### Propaganda efforts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Propaganda efforts")]

During this period Goulooze acted to ensure that [communist propaganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_propaganda "Communist propaganda") in the form of the newspapers _Op de bon_ and _Het Panster_ reached every part of the [Royal Netherlands Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Netherlands_Army "Royal Netherlands Army"). A special propaganda stunt was the publication of military booklet by the officer Jan Zonderland, that contained a worker's oath. The case gained national attention, due the commotion from baggage searches in barracks to remove it; that it came to the notice of the national press, the daily newspaper _Het Leven_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198071%E2%80%9372-25)

### Reforming the International Workers Aid

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Reforming the International Workers Aid")]

In 1930, the [International Workers Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workers_International_Relief "Workers International Relief") (IAH, Internationale Arbeiders hulp) that existed to provide aid to strikers and strengthen cultural ties with the Soviet Union, became embroiled in a disagreement amongst its members, that degenerated into a fight. Goulooze was ordered to take over the reconstruction of the IAH and oversee the election of a new board.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198073-26)

### CPN Board member

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: CPN Board member")]

The [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") exacerbated the political problems faced by the CPN. The Comintern believed it would result in revolution in the Netherlands. Members of the CPN were in favour of the Comintern attitude, that saw Social Democrats, the main political fulcrum of the ruling class, as the main obstacle to the establishment of a proletarian revolution.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198075%E2%80%9376-27) The Comintern classed them as _"social fascists"_ who had to be fought at all costs; they were the enemy. Goulooze, who was centrist, rejected this view. At a meeting at his house on 1 February 1930, [Richard Gyptner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Gyptner "Richard Gyptner") of the [Young Communist International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Communist_International "Young Communist International"), castigated him for this. After a long discussion, the Young Communist League board decided to support the Comintern position. At that point, Goulooze ended his association with the Young Communist League and he was tasked along with four others to organise a conference of CPN members.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198078-28)

## In service to the Comintern

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In service to the Comintern")]

In February 1930, a new board was elected at the conference and the membership achieved unity on the basis of political guidelines received from the Comintern. At the age of 24, Goulooze became a member of the CPN and was elected as a CPN board member. He became the secretary of the youth organisation, a position he held for four years.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198079%E2%80%9380-29)

Goulooze was then subsequently elected organisational secretary of the CPN.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198080-30) During this period, it was requested by the party leadership that Goulooze should write on his thoughts and views, now he had a better understanding of the internal functioning of the party. He tried to identify those who are not following the Stalinist line and advocated for stronger control of party members.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198081%E2%80%9382-31)

### Publishing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Publishing")]

Goulooze was given the task of publishing communist brochures and books. His love of writing up to that point was known in the Party and he achieved a level of published work for the organisation that has not been reached since.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198083-32)

In 1927, he wrote _De grondslagen van het communisme, de taak van de_ (_the foundations of communism, the task of the communist youth_), followed by the 104 page essay on the 1928 KJI Congress.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198083-32) Goulooze considered reading and studying a revolutionary act. Over the next several years, he built up publishing arm of the CPN and imported communist literature from abroad. He also opened a number of communist bookshops.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198084-33)

In 1933, he established the _Amstel Agency_, a publishing house that was run by Lydia Wolters, his wife. The publishing work was done in his own house. During the early 1930s, he made numerous trips abroad to arrange contracts with writers.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198084-33) In 1932, he published a book by N. Bogdanov, _Het eerste meisje; een romantische geschiedenis_ (_The first girl; a romantic history_), about life for members in the [Komsomol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komsomol "Komsomol").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198085-34) In March 1934, as the work of publishing at his house was becoming too stressful due to the success of the business, Goulooze established the formal _Pegasus_ publishing house, located at 29 Nieuwe Prinsengracht in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"). During the course of his work as director, he formed relationships with many leading [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing "Left-wing") intellectuals and new writers and academics in the country.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198085%E2%80%9389-35) During the period he worked there, Goulooze published _[The ABC of Communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_ABC\_of\_Communism "The ABC of Communism")_ written by [Nikolai Bukharin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Bukharin "Nikolai Bukharin") and [Yevgeni Preobrazhensky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yevgeni_Preobrazhensky "Yevgeni Preobrazhensky") and the _Marxist Library_ in 24 volumes. These were classic works by writers like [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx"), [Friedrich Engels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Engels "Friedrich Engels"), [Vladimir Lenin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Lenin "Vladimir Lenin") and [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin"). These books were generally not available in the [Dutch language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language") beforehand, so they sold in large quantities.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198087-36) Among the most important people who ran his publishing house was Hein Kohn, the main driving force in the publishing house as well as Nel Schuitemaker, Martien Beversluis, and Menno Poldervaart.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198089-37)
