In 1933, after the uprising in the [Royal Netherlands Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Netherlands_Navy "Royal Netherlands Navy")[coastal defence ship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_defence_ship "Coastal defence ship")[HNLMS De Zeven Provinciën](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HNLMS_De_Zeven_Provinci%C3%ABn_(1909) "HNLMS De Zeven Provinciën (1909)"), the Dutch government banned a whole series of left-wing organisations including the CPN.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198091-40) This brought huge scrutiny to the CPN and Goulooze as secretary was made responsible for the security of the organisation. Over the next few months, he built a network of trusted people that were committed to identifying and stopping infiltration by the police, the [Centrale Inlichtingendienst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrale_Inlichtingendienst?action=edit&redlink=1 "Centrale Inlichtingendienst (page does not exist)")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) and other intelligence agencies.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198091-40) Through that work, he became familiar with many members of the Belgian and French Communist parties and the Comintern.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198093-41)

### Reichstag fire

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Reichstag fire")]

On 30 January 1933, Hitler became [Chancellor of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_Germany "Chancellor of Germany") and following the [Reichstag fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichstag_fire "Reichstag fire") on 27 February 1933, strengthened his power. The communists and the CPN believed Hitler would fail, in the expectation that they would come to power.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198095-42) Instead, Hitler used the fire as a pretext to launch an attack on Communist and Bolshevist groups in Germany in an attempt to destroy them.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198096-43) At the time, Goulooze was in Berlin and met Georgi Dimitrov, who had been arrested, after being seen talking to [Marinus van der Lubbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marinus_van_der_Lubbe "Marinus van der Lubbe"), who was accused of starting the fire. Goulooze provided information to Dimitrov that ensured his release. Goulooze used the opportunity to print [The Brown Book of the Reichstag Fire and Hitler Terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Brown_Book_of_the_Reichstag_Fire_and_Hitler_Terror "The Brown Book of the Reichstag Fire and Hitler Terror"), in the Netherlands that placed the blame for the fire with the Nazis.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen198098-44)

In the summer of 1933, Goulooze provided assistance to [Johann Wenzel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wenzel "Johann Wenzel"), a [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRU_(G.U.) "GRU (G.U.)") agent and radio operator who was part of a Soviet espionage group that operated in Western Europe.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeberHerbstWenzel2008-45) Wenzel travelled to the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") with [Theodor Bottländer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodor_Bottl%C3%A4nder?action=edit&redlink=1 "Theodor Bottländer (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodor%20Bottl%C3%A4nder "de:Theodor Bottländer")], a German official of the [AM-Apparat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimilit%C3%A4rischer_Apparat "Antimilitärischer Apparat") department of the Central Committee of the KPD, to obtain information on [Marinus van der Lubbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marinus_van_der_Lubbe "Marinus van der Lubbe").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeberHerbstWenzel2008-45)

### International Red Aid

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: International Red Aid")]

The [International Red Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Red_Aid "International Red Aid") (MOPR) was an international social service organization established by the [Communist International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_International "Communist International") in 1922.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazi%C4%871986xxviii-46) When the Nazis came to power at the end of January 1933, hundreds of German communists made a direct appeal to the MOPR for help. In 1933, it became clear the MOPR was insufficient in design and strength to deal with the number of people who were applying for help. The CPN instructed Jan Postma to expand the organisation.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980103-47)

At the end of 1933, it was given a higher workload when it moved to larger rooms at the [Bloemgracht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloemgracht "Bloemgracht") in Amsterdam. It was manned by Piet de Smit who did the secretarial work, [Anton Winterink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Winterink "Anton Winterink"), who was part of the editorial work, and Friedl Baruch, who became the KPD liaison.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5)

Goulooze along with Winterink and many others members of the CPN were involved in raising aid money to buy food and clothing for the refugees[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980106-48) at a time when police were actively hostile to the refugees and the banned CPN.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980106-48) The CPN had many enemies outwith the Dutch state and the police, that included enemy agents posing as communists seeking help but there to infiltrate the CPN. That led to the arrest of many genuine communists. Postma worked closely with Goulooze and became responsible for checking the reliability of each refugee in turn.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980114-49) Goulooze's job was to protect the organisation particularly from espionage attempts and the police.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5)

In 1934, the [Communist Party of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Germany "Communist Party of Germany") (KPD) established an underground bureau, known as an _Abschnittsleitungen_ in Amsterdam.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980115-50) Goulooze arranged for communists who were working on KPD assignments to travel between the Netherlands and Germany. In the summer of 1939, the relationship between the CPN and KPD deteriorated due to the [Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact "Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980120-51) By May 1940 and the [German invasion of the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_invasion_of_the_Netherlands "German invasion of the Netherlands"), the relationship between the two organisation had completely broken down. Goulooze was the only person to maintain contact with the illegal KPD leadership in Amsterdam.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980123-52)

### Comintern

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Comintern")]

In the period immediately after the Nazis seized power on 30 January 1933, Goulooze made several trips to the Soviet Union, Prague and Paris in the context of reorganising the Comintern.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980123-52) In the same year, the [International Liaison Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Liaison_Department_(Comintern) "International Liaison Department (Comintern)") (OMS) of the Comintern[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Sullivan2010259-53) was transferred from Berlin to Amsterdam[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980125-54) under the command of [Osip Piatnitsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osip_Piatnitsky "Osip Piatnitsky") in Amsterdam. [[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980124-55) The OMS was a part legal, part illegal organisation whose purpose was to carry out administrative policy including arranging travel for officials, to develop and maintain a communication system between the Comintern and the Soviet Union using radio communications and couriers, as well as managing funding for the Comintern organisation and to care for wealthy communists.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980124-55) Goulooze provided the addresses where the Comintern radio transmitters could be housed in Amsterdam.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980125-54) In 1934, Bulgarian Communist leader [Georgi Dimitrov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgi_Dimitrov "Georgi Dimitrov") was elected secretary of the Comintern and Goulooze became further involved in the daily running of the organisation.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980123-52)

In 1935, with permission from the CPN, he started working primarily for the Comintern, but remained director of the _Pegasus_ publishing house, that he used for cover.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979281-1) In the same period, between 1935 and 1937, Dutch CPN member, August Johannes van Proosdy was recruited by Goulooze and sent for technical training in wireless telegraphy techniques in the Soviet Union.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197957-56)

### Dutch Information Service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Dutch Information Service")]

By 1937, he was completely devolved from the CPN executive.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980123-52) In the same year, Goulooze was ordered by Dimitrov to disband the current OMS in Amsterdam and create a new OMS, with the infrastructure to support communications with Moscow, including new radio operators, electricians and couriers that were to be recruited from the CPN.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980125-54)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197969-57) It was completely separate from the former German Comintern.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980125-54)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197969-57) Goulooze was provided help by Wenzel, who moved to the Netherlands, in early 1937. Wenzel was an expert radio engineer and they discussed plans for the construction of a radio network in the Netherlands.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979383-58)

As a publisher Goulooze, was able to travel widely without restrictions, that enabled him to meet a wide variety of people, and select particular people for particular jobs.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980123-52) In the same year, he received intelligence training at the [Marx–Engels–Lenin Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marx%E2%80%93Engels%E2%80%93Lenin_Institute "Marx–Engels–Lenin Institute") in Moscow.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) By April 1939, van Proosdy had built a radio transmitter that was based on the [Hartley oscillator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartley_oscillator "Hartley oscillator"). Goulooze knew nothing of how wireless telegraphy worked, so delegated the [ciphering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cipher "Cipher") and radio transmission to his employees.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980127-59)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-61)

In June 1939, Goulooze recruited Adam Nagel, a photographer[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197966-62) and communist member of the CPN to work with Wenzel in Belgium.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197958-63) In the same period Goulooze recruited CPN member Jacobus "Co" Dankaart as his deputy in the information service and became the group's treasurer. Dankaart also worked as a [cutout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutout_(espionage) "Cutout (espionage)") between the radio group and Goulooze.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197958-63)

### Non aggression pact

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Non aggression pact")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Winterink_Group.png/250px-Winterink_Group.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Winterink_Group.png)

The Winterink Group in the Netherlands. It was also known as Group _Hilda_

The [Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact "Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact") signed in August 1939, defined neutrality between the ideological rivals of Germany and the Soviet Union. However, it created considerable ideological difficulties for the CPN and the Comintern. The Comintern pursued no policy other than what the Soviet government planned. It labeled the global conflagration as an imperialist conflict and rejected the pact.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980132%E2%80%93133-64)

With the coming of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the ideology of [Popular Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Front "Popular Front") and [United front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_front "United front") were abandoned by communist parties in Europe, and the politics of proletarian class struggle once again became predominant. The [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party") were no longer called to defend the French homeland when France declared war on Germany, so was declared a proscribed organisation. [[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980133-65)

The French government began to persecute Communists in France, leaving the French Comintern, the KPD and Communist Party is disarray.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980133-65) This resulted in Goulooze's organisation becoming increasingly important to Soviet intelligence as the only organisation in Western Europe that could maintain contact with agents on the ground.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979282-6) In the Netherlands, the leadership of the CPN was expanded to cope with the _supposed_ increased work, in fact it was to attempt to balance opposing ideologies on the board.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980135-66) The leadership of the CPN eventually began to disagree with the leadership of the Comintern, their viewpoint becoming diametrically opposed. While the CPN viewed the war as a fight between opposing ideologies, the Comintern believed it was a true power struggle between nations.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980137-67)

### Soviet intelligence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Soviet intelligence")]

In October 1939, [Anatoly Gurevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Gurevich "Anatoly Gurevich"), a Ukrainian [GRU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Intelligence_Directorate_(GRU) "Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU)") agent who was part of a Soviet espionage group that operated in Germany, and Belgium, visited Goulooze to request help to build his espionage network in Belgium.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) Gurevich asked that a temporary wireless telegraphy link be established for his use, while he established his own wireless telegraphy link in Belgian and this was provided by Goulooze and used, until January 1940.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) In July 1940, Gurevich again visited Goulooze, his second visit, to request the reserve cypher code,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-68) that Goulooze had received from his visit to the Soviet Union, the year before.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2)

## Occupation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Occupation")]

After the [occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_in_World_War_II "Netherlands in World War II") of the Netherlands by the Wehrmacht that began on 10 May 1940, a meeting was held by the CPN on 15 May 1940, where it was realised that many of the members would not survive the war and the party itself would have to operate illegally.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980137-67) The secretariat was reformed with many members put in reserve with Paul De Groot, [Jan Dieters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Dieters?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jan Dieters (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan%20Dieters "nl:Jan Dieters")] and [Lou Jansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Jansen_(verzetsstrijder)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lou Jansen (verzetsstrijder) (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou%20Jansen%20(verzetsstrijder) "nl:Lou Jansen (verzetsstrijder)")] forming the triumvirate that gradually brought the illegal CPN into action. During that month, De Groot planned to run the illegal CPN from Moscow and was in contact with Goulooze to arrange passage by ship, but the plan was abandoned when De Groot and Goulooze visited the Soviet trade representative in Netherlands who rejected the idea. [[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980140-69)

De Groot then expounded the idea of editing and printing an illegal newspaper from [Vichy France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France"). Goulooze explored the idea with French and Belgian communists but the plan was found to be impractical and was abandoned. De Groot instructed Goulooze to contact the Comintern executive in Moscow, to make a request for the secretariat to move to Moscow but on 21 June 1940, Dimitrov rejected the idea, informing De Groot that the group had stay in the Netherlands. Dimitrov forwarded detailed instructions to the secretariat on how to resist the occupation.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980140-69)

The members of the secretariat

[![Image 16: Paul De Groot](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Paul_de_Groot_%28kop%29%2C_Bestanddeelnr_920-1109.jpg/250px-Paul_de_Groot_%28kop%29%2C_Bestanddeelnr_920-1109.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_de_Groot_(kop),_Bestanddeelnr_920-1109.jpg)

Paul De Groot in 1967.

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Lou-jansen-1427492419.jpg/250px-Lou-jansen-1427492419.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lou-jansen-1427492419.jpg)

Lou Jansen in 1943.

During the first months of the occupation, individual leaders of the CPN lacked a cohesive approach to resisting the occupation and took a wait-and-see approach on the political front. Goulooze used to time he was contact with the CPN leadership to call for more political activity.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980141-70) From the very beginning Goulooze was in favour of uncompromising and vigorous resistance to the Germans.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5)

During this period, Goulooze was reporting to the Comintern. [[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980141-70) The reports were created by the CPN party leadership. Due to the limited radio contact, he would first send the reports in an abbreviated form, as well as forwarding each completed report to Moscow by courier.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980141-70) In October 1940, the secretariat complained to Goulooze about a summary letter that Goulooze had written, that was critical of the secretariat, of its wait-and-see approach. In a meeting of the CPN leadership, they decided to replace him after holding a vote that resulted in "no confidence". The secretariat had withdrawn from Amsterdam, leaving the OMS in the city.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980142-71)

Goulooze had stated in the letter than they should have maintained more contact with the OMS in city. The secretariat failed to understand that Goulooze was employed by the Comintern executive directly from Moscow, and had no control over him. De Groot contacted the Comintern executive, who dismissed the idea of replacing him and demanded from that point forward all messages meant for the executive go through Goulooze.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980142-71)

### Collaboration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Collaboration")]

On 24 June 1940, the Dutch government withdrew the CPN publication ban and on 26 June an issue of the "[Volksdagblad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Waarheid "De Waarheid")"[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-73) was written.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980137-67) In an article, [Paul de Groot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Groot "Paul de Groot") opined that German aggression was caused by English imperialism and the Dutch [bourgeoisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeoisie "Bourgeoisie"), stating that the [Dutch people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people") had no "enmity" towards the German people and that the Dutch people had "only an interest in friendship and peace with the German people".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980137-67) The article went on by stating:

"It is in the highest interest of the Dutch population that they neither directly nor indirectly, support the warfare of the Allies, but that they observe a true neutrality towards Germany. Restoring peace and friendship with the German people is the first step that the Dutch people can and must take in the interest of restoring general peace. This also means that the Dutch working people must adopt a correct attitude towards the German occupation of our country"[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980138-74)
Goulooze read the "Volksdagblad" article and was vehemently opposed to its printing. He managed to make contact with a Comintern representative, who contacted the Comintern executive in Moscow. They forbade its printing. However, the article was released. At the time, there was some panic in the CPN at the release of the article and how it would be viewed.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980138-74) It did not prevent the CPN and its organs from being banned by the [Arthur Seyss-Inquart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Seyss-Inquart "Arthur Seyss-Inquart") in July 1940.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEForay201266-75)

### Expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Expansion")]

At the beginning of the occupation, Goulooze had recruited one radio engineer, van Proosdy, whose codename was "Frans".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980143-76) The transmitter was hidden in van Proosdy's house in Orteliusstraat in Amsterdam.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) In 1938, CPN member Jan de Laar was recruited by Goulooze and sent to the Soviet Union for technical training in wireless telegraphy and intelligence techniques. When de Laar returned he became an assistant to van Proosdy.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2)

In April 1940, van Proosdy built a radio transmitter for use by a woman in south Amsterdam and by February 1941, she had been trained to use it.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980145-77) In total, five radio operators were eventually recruited by Goulooze by the end of 1941.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980143-76) To ensure a high level of security, Goulooze separated the encryption/decryption of messages by the cypher clerks from the radio transmission process and used couriers to move messages around, with messages hidden in matchboxes, flashlight batteries or rolled in cigarette cases. It resulted in the radio operator's never knowing what the contents of their message were and the cypher clerks not knowing who transmitted the telegrams.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980146-78) At the same time, the people in his network were employed in legitimate roles designed to disguise their illegal activity, for example as municipal workers.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980146-78)

Goulooze used low-power [shortwave radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortwave_radio "Shortwave radio") transmitters that used the 30-metre band (10.100–10.150 MHz) and that were capable of long-distance traffic.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980147-79) The transmission of telegrams took place at different times. As the war progressed, Goulooze passed on messages from the KPD, the CPN and the Comintern. Information on military activity, e.g. armaments, deployment of units along with industrial activity, e.g. production figures, was increasingly also collected and forwarded.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980147-79)

### Request for help

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Request for help")]

In the summer of 1941, [Eugen Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_Fried "Eugen Fried") contacted Goulooze to request his help to expand his radio network in Brussels.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980149-80) Goulooze sent van Proosdy to Brussels in August 1941. van Proosdy was shown a self-built transmitter by the young person who was hosting it, but it refused to work. A new transmitter was delivered by courier to van Proosdy, three weeks later and he managed to make a connection to Moscow.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980151-81)

### CPN Resolve

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: CPN Resolve")]

As the CPN recovered after being banned, a second meeting of the triumvirate was arranged in July 1940, where they updated and prepared new manifestos. They decided to force a general strike in the large metal companies in November and protest against the persecution of Jews. At the end of November, the CPN published an edition of the _[De Waarheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_Waarheid "De Waarheid")_ (_The Truth_).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980152-7)

Goulooze considered the actions too late and was annoyed that the newspaper did not mention the CPN itself.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980153-82) Goulooze, who was in communication with the comintern, was critical of the strike.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980154-83) The comintern sent instructions to direct the goals of the CPN, i.e. not to see their work as proletarian revolution but as a national liberation struggle. The editorials that later appeared in the future versions of the De Waarheid, made the point in clear language, stating it was not about communism, it was about national liberation and return of democratic freedoms.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980156-84) Despite the friction between Goulooze and the executive, the CPN leadership still used Goulooze to pass messages to the Comintern.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980157-85)

### Red Orchestra

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Red Orchestra")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/95/Organisation_of_the_KPD_in_1942.png/250px-Organisation_of_the_KPD_in_1942.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Organisation_of_the_KPD_in_1942.png)

Organisation of the KPD in 1942, showing the lines of communication and the command hierarchy

Main article: [Red Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Orchestra_(espionage) "Red Orchestra (espionage)")

Much more important for the Soviet Union than the CPN and the triumvirate, was the work undertaken by Goulooze for the KPD.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980157-85) From the outset of the war, Goulooze maintained radio links between the area control centre ("Abschnittsleitung") of the KPD in Amsterdam and the area control centre of the KPD in Paris, the Western European Bureau of the Comintern in Paris and Comintern Executive in Moscow.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980172-86) He also managed the links between the Abschnittsleitung in Amsterdam and illegal groups in Germany. [[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980172-86) In 1939, the French KPD groups fell into disarray as the French government banned the [French communist party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_communist_party "French communist party") and interned many of its members.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980172-86) As a result, radio and courier services were cut. The Comintern used Goulooze to bring these various groups back into contact with each other.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980172-86)

### Knöchel Emigre group

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Knöchel Emigre group")]

At a meeting in Moscow in 1940, it was decided that the various KPD Abschnittsleitung in different capitals in Germany should be dissolved, to enable the formation of a new operational leadership in Germany.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980173-87) The intention was for German KPD organiser, [Wilhelm Knöchel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Kn%C3%B6chel "Wilhelm Knöchel")[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-89) to take change of the KPD in Germany.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980173-87)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2009270-90) Knöchel who was considered an exceptionally effective communist resistance organiser, whose alias was "Alfred".[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGebauer2011496%E2%80%93501-91) He had been living in Amsterdam since 1936 and was the leader of an emigre group of German communists. By 1939, he was living in Moscow and was a full member of the Central Committee of the KPD.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeberHerbstKn%C3%B6chel2008-92)

To bring this plan into operation, the Comintern decided the planning stage would be done in Amsterdam, which resulted in Knöchel returning to Amsterdam. Together with [Willi Gall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willi_Gall "Willi Gall"), Knöchel began publishing communist literature that included various leaflets and bulletins, for example "The Enemy Stands in Your Own Country", for distribution in Berlin.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980173-87) From mid-1940, Knöchel with the assistance of Goulooze began to train the emigre group of communists in the Netherlands to work in Germany as political activists and informers.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197971-88) Goulooze was able to obtain blank identity cards, along with official stamps from a colleague that enabled the KPD members who were hiding, to interact with CPN members in Amsterdam and to travel safely to Germany in some cases under [diplomatic protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_protection "Diplomatic protection"). At the time, Goulooze received instructions from the Comintern and Swedish Communist Party in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm")[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980173%E2%80%9374-93) where the KPD leadership emigrated after they were banned. As the Swedish communists were against setting up a radio transmitter link with Amsterdam, Goulooze organised a courier link by sea and when the sailors visited the sea port of [Delfzijl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delfzijl "Delfzijl"), he would pick up a suitcase full of communist brochures, magazines and other literature. In that manner, the Dutch CPN and KPD members managed to read the latest Russian communist literature. The connection by sea, broke down in late 1941 or early 1942 when many Swiss communists were arrested.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980174%E2%80%9375-94)

The first KPD member to travel to Germany with Goulooze's identity documents was [Alfons Kaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfons_Kaps?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alfons Kaps (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfons%20Kaps "de:Alfons Kaps")] who went as an instructor, in January 1941. The next person to travel was [Willi Seng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willi_Seng "Willi Seng"). Albert Kamradt was the third person. The fourth person was [Alfred Kowalke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kowalke?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alfred Kowalke (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred%20Kowalke "de:Alfred Kowalke")].[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980178-95) On the 9 January 1942, Knöchel met Goulooze for a final meeting before travelling to Germany, taking along blank identity papers, a selection of official stamps and communist literature, travelling as an itinerant silver polisher. [[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980179-96) At the time, Goulooze arranged for everything that was published by the Comintern executive in Moscow, to be couriered to Knöchel in Berlin.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980181-97) When he arrived in Berlin, Knöchel started to produce the [hectographed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectograph "Hectograph") "Der Friedenskämpfer" (“The Fighter for Peace,”) that offered detailed accounts of German atrocities across the [eastern front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Front_(World_War_II) "Eastern Front (World War II)").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson2009270-90) The May 1942 special edition of "Der Friedenskämpfer" included detailed knowledge of the execution of French, Czechs, Germans, and Norwegians across Europe and as well as specific military companies that carried out executions of Soviet POWs in Leningrad, and civilians in [Lviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv "Lviv"). Knöchel exchanged documents in the form of micro-photocopies with [Elisabeth Schumacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Schumacher "Elisabeth Schumacher").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson200971-98) and [Wilhelm Guddorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Guddorf "Wilhelm Guddorf") who were the intermediaries of [John Sieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Sieg "John Sieg"). It is not known if Sieg ever met Knöchel.

When Knöchel left for Germany, at least 10 communist instructors still had to be recruited and sent to Germany.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99) Arranging the travelling for the instructors became increasingly difficult, due to heavy bombing and increased German security, leaving only a river connection. The difficulty was the lines of radio communication between from the KPD in Germany, to Goulooze DIS and onwards to the Comintern in Moscow.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99) At the time, Knöchel was using two couriers, his common-law wife [Cilly Hansmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Hansmann?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cecilia Hansmann (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A4cilie%20Hansmann "de:Cäcilie Hansmann")], and [Charlotte Garske](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Garske "Charlotte Garske") to move intelligence between Berlin and Amsterdam for transmission to the Comintern. In the late summer 1942, the Comintern and the KPD leadership through [Wilhelm Pieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Pieck "Wilhelm Pieck") began to urge Goulooze to establish a radio communication link in Berlin. Considered an extremely perilous and difficult task, Goulooze selected van Proosdy for this. [[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99)

Van Proosdy had to establish a legal existence in Germany by registering with the _[Arbeitseinsatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbeitseinsatz "Arbeitseinsatz")_. Once that was completed, it was arranged for a letter to be sent by Willem Visser, an employee of a small Berlin based electricity company that was part of [AEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEG_(German_company) "AEG (German company)"), to offer a position of employment to Van Proosdy, as an electrician. [[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99) Van Proosdy left on 2 December 1942, using documentation arranged by Goulooze. In Berlin, he made contact with Knöchel, who introduced him to Kowalke who was to be trained as a radio operator.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980182-99) Goulooze arranged for a radio transmitter to be sent by ship but it never arrived. He then forwarded a small reserve transmitter by ship as a replacement.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980183-100)

### Soviet Parachutists

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Soviet Parachutists")]

[![Image 19](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/KRUYT%2C_John_William.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KRUYT,_John_William.jpg)

Jan Wilhelm Kruyt, who was arrested after parachuting from a plane and breaking his leg

In 1942, Goulooze arranged with Soviet intelligence to recruit new radio operators. These were agents that were part of [Operation Pickaxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Pickaxe?action=edit&redlink=1 "Operation Pickaxe (page does not exist)")[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTETyas2017106-101) and dropped by aircraft sent from [RAF Tempsford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Tempsford "RAF Tempsford"). In early 1942, Goulooze arranged to receive Soviet parachutists by delegating an area close to a body of water in [Veluwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veluwe "Veluwe"), where they could be safely accommodated.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980169-102) On 22 June 1942, Jan Wilhelm Kruyt Jr, was parachuted into the Netherlands with a wireless telegraphy set for Goulooze and false papers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2) On 24 June 1942, [Jan Wilhelm Kruyt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Kruyt "Willy Kruyt") Sr, an ardent communist and ex-clergyman was dropped by parachute from a British plane in Belgium.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980170-103) Kruyt Sr broke his leg when he landed and was arrested shortly after by the [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo "Gestapo") and sent to [Fort Breendonk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Breendonk "Fort Breendonk").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979303-104) On 30 November, a Soviet agent [Peter Kousnetzov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kousnetzov?action=edit&redlink=1 "Peter Kousnetzov (page does not exist)") using the alias Bruno Kühn was parachuted into the Netherlands.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197970-2)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980171-105) Kousnetzov was found by Goulooze's men after wandering about the woods for a night.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980171-105) Kousnetzov was originally sent to provide support the Knöchel network in Germany.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197971-88) However, Goulooze was unable to contact Knöchel at the time, so decided to contact the Comintern executive to request that Kousnetzov work with CPN radio operator Jan de Laar instead, which was agreed. Kousnetzov joined De Laar in March 1943 and worked to train agents in the Netherlands to work inside Germany.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris197971-88)

## Sonderkommando Rote Kapelle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Sonderkommando Rote Kapelle")]

On 18 or 19 August 1942 (sources vary), Winterink was arrested[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979389-106)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStadsarchief_AmsterdamInventory_of_the_archives_of_Riek_Milikowski-de_Raat-107) by the [Sonderkommando Rote Kapelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonderkommando_Rote_Kapelle "Sonderkommando Rote Kapelle") at a cafe in Amsterdam, after being betrayed by [Konstantin Jeffremov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstantin_Jeffremov "Konstantin Jeffremov").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStadsarchief_AmsterdamInventory_of_the_archives_of_Riek_Milikowski-de_Raat-107)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKesaris1979389-106) Nine members of the group with two remaining radios were not discovered and continued to work. A total of 17 people from Winterink's group were arrested. This arrests led to an unpleasant aftermath for Goulooze as rumours were spread by the CPN that it was Goulooze's fault.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980169-102) Winterink's friends even went as far in stating that Goulooze was a member of the [Sicherheitsdienst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicherheitsdienst "Sicherheitsdienst").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980169-102) Due to the rumours, distrust in Goulooze grew to an extent that it was decided by two members of the CPN, Ab Arendse and Piet Groeneveld to kill Goulooze. When their preparations were complete, they contacted Jan Postma, who decided to intervene to prevent the execution.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980169-102)

### Search for Goulooze

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Search for Goulooze")]

On 12 January 1943, Alfons Kaps was arrested by the Sonderkommando [[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980185-108) in [Düsseldorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCsseldorf "Düsseldorf"), following a denunciation.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGebauer2011237-109) Under enhanced torture, he agreed to work for the Sonderkommando as a [double agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_agent "Double agent") or V-Mann,[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-111) first betraying Willi Seng, who was arrested on 20 January 1943 and who was also subject to enhanced torture.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeberHerbst2008-112) After the indictment, Kaps took his own life in March 1943.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980185-108) Through Seng, Knöchel was betrayed and was arrested on 30 January 1943.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980186-113) After he was tortured, Knöchel agreed to become a V-Mann and held a number of meetings with van Proosdy in the normal course of operation, making him effectively under the control of the Gestapo. Van Proosdy eventually realised that Knöchel was a V-Mann, due to his general demeanor and errant behaviour. He decided to make arrangements to return to Amsterdam but was arrested on 22 May 1943 before he could leave. Upon learning from a contact that van Proosdy was arrested and that the Sonderkommando was searching for him, Goulooze went into hiding.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980187-114)

The Sonderkommando first attempted to use van Proosdy's wife in a trick to expose him, but this was unsuccessful. Even when the Gestapo managed to find a photograph of Goulooze, they were unable to locate him.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980187%E2%80%93188-115) By 10 June 1943, Goulooze had informed all his radio and cipher people that it was likely van Proosdy was arrested and that they should go into hiding.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1988a-5) At the time, all the work and residual addresses were abandoned.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980187%E2%80%93189-116) On the night of 1–2 July 1943, the Gestapo raided all the addresses they had been monitoring and suspected, but it yielded nothing of importance. However, on 2 July, the Gestapo arrested one of Goulooze's radio operators. [[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980190-117) The man was tortured and revealed that he was to meet Goulooze's deputy, Jacobus Dankaart, the next afternoon. However the Gestapo bungled the meeting and the Dankaart was shot twice in the back when he tried to flee.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980191-118) By the end of July several more of the radio people had been arrested and two of the radio sets had been captured by the Sonderkommando. Goulooze informed the Comintern in Moscow through the last transmitter of the situation, that the OMS group would be disbanded.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980192-119) On the 24 August 1943, Dankaart was taken to the Zuidwal hospital in The Hague.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980195-120) This enabled Goulooze to contact Dankaart to arrange an escape plan, which was successful on 18 September 1943.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980196-121) During the following days, the Gestapo operation continued. Comintern agent [Eugen Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_Fried "Eugen Fried") (Clément), Goulooze's collaborator and liaison with the French Communist Party was shot dead in Brussels on 17 August 1943.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980197-122) On the 5 November 1943, Kowalke was executed. During his many months of interrogation, he never exposed any names, which saved the lives of many people in Goulooze's organisation. [[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980198-123) Another close collaborator of Goulooze was [Erich Gentsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Gentsch?action=edit&redlink=1 "Erich Gentsch (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich%20Gentsch "de:Erich Gentsch")] who was the director of the KPD in Amsterdam since 1936. He was arrested in April 1943 and never exposed any names during his interrogation over many months.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980199-124) He was hanged in August 1944.

### Dissolution of the Comintern

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Dissolution of the Comintern")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/928.Joseph_E._Davies_1939.jpg/250px-928.Joseph_E._Davies_1939.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:928.Joseph_E._Davies_1939.jpg)

The American diplomat [Joseph E. Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_E._Davies "Joseph E. Davies") who did so much to disguise the true nature of Stalinist Russia

On the 15 May 1943, Goulooze was listening to the radio broadcasts from Moscow, when he heard that the Comintern had been dissolved on the order of Stalin.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980201-125) For Goulooze, who was a revolutionary, the vision that the Comintern presented was one of a need for world revolution. Harmsen posits that Goulooze must have been disappointed and even expressed some doubt about the value of the work that he had done for the organisation up to that point[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980203-126) but ultimately his revolutionary zeal wouldn't have been extinguished.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Goulooze#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarmsen1980203-126) Goulooze wouldn't have known about the [Stalinist purges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge") that started in August 1936. He came to know about the [trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_of_the_Anti-Soviet_%22Bloc_of_Rightists_and_Trotskyites%22 "Case of the Anti-Soviet \"Bloc of Rightists and Trotskyites\"") of the group associated with [Leon Trotsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Trotsky "Leon Trotsky") after several Comintern officials whom he had met when he visited the Soviet Union and spoke to on the radio were replaced and this swayed his ideology to such an extent that he had a real fear of [Trotskyism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trotskyism "Trotskyism"). He came to know about it through a copy of the memoir by the American diplomat [Joseph E. Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_E._Davies "Joseph E. By: Jaclyn A. Smith Submitted as a fulfillment of the requirements for the Masters of Arts Degree in History The University of Toledo December, 2007 D.W. Griffith capitalized upon already existing theories and social positions in order to present audiences with entertaining plots and dramatic antagonists. Often these subjects consisted of individuals that were potentially marketable regarding public opinion and sensationalism, allowing him to make a name for himself in the film world as a source of artistic and technical innovations. Perhaps known best for his controversial film, Birth of a Nation,1 he has been applauded and crucified by modern historians and analysts regarding his creative practices and basically, spread of racial stereotypes to early film audiences. The denigration of his work by modern scholars lies mainly within the characters and racial tensions that were perpetuated on-screen as a result of his conceptual character options. However, in many of his early films that were produced at the Biograph Company, Griffith initiated exposure for gender, racial and ethnic groups that were largely ignored and propelled these issues to the  

> 1 The Birth of a Nation in Griffith Masterworks , DVD, directed by D.W. Griffith (NY: Kino Video, 2002/1915).

iv 

forefront of the public eye. Griffith should be celebrated as a filmmaker that used controversy to provoke thought regarding issues of race, class and gender, and certainly his other films have the teaching capability that Birth of a Nation is commonly utilized for. There are several other pieces that were produced by Griffith that are symbolic of public attitudes and accurate representation of society near the turn of the twentieth century. These works should be celebrated as primary resource materials, and therefore used in classrooms to teach political, racial and social issues to students that wish to study such concepts. The evidence for this theory lies not only in his films, but in the behind-the-scenes production occurrences, character references, personal anecdotes and various current and past media sources. The documentation that will be employed in order to support this thesis follow in the form of original film reviews, newspaper articles detailing public reaction, governmental law, biographical and autobiographical information, periodicals, essays and finally this author’s examination of the gender, moral, racially and ethnically based films released under D.W. Griffith from 1908 to 1919 that have survived through documentation or independently. v

Introduction The utilization of visual aids in a classroom is invaluable as a result of the different learning styles preferred by individual students. Before documentaries and fictional films, students were relied upon still photographs, drawings, maps and words in order to link a visual impression with a body of text. Throughout the twentieth century, film has emerged as an important teaching tool that allows students the experience of actually seeing an occurrence or event either as it happened, or they are able to view a creative representation of the occasion, in regard to fictional depictions. Despite the immense body of work that D.W. Griffith produced between 1908 and 1940, educators usually focus on one controversial film in particular. Birth of a Nation2 is a widely-taught piece in upper-level history courses throughout the U.S. Several reputable institutions, including Virginia Tech’s department of Teaching and Learning use this in various parts of their curriculum to impress upon those that are studying to become teachers the importance of visual aids in instructional situations. At Virginia Tech, Dr. Dave Hicks uses Birth of a Nation to satisfy the National Social Studies Content Standards/expectations and indicates that the film is an apt tool to satisfy the standards that fall under the “Time, Continuity and Change”    

> 2Birth of a Nation, in Griffith Masterworks , DVD, directed by D.W. Griffith (NY: Kino Video, 2002/1915).

2

category, as well as provide insight for students as to general media influences on individuals throughout time.3 The film is memorable for its graphic violence, alleged glorification of the Klu Klux Klan, and notoriously anti-African American portrayals and stereotypes. Interestingly enough, until the aftermath of World War II, despite the controversy that this film caused, Griffith was applauded for his innovative film techniques, and credited with establishing Birth of a Nation as the first feature-length film. 4 As a result of growing intolerance at the turn of the twentieth century regarding race, gender and ethnicity in the United States, as well as the civil rights movement, recent public and critical opinions regarding Griffith’s character have gone sour. Birth of a Nation , is primarily viewed as an appropriate teaching vehicle for adult or high school education purposes, due to the graphic and emotional scenes that are presented. Sadly, Griffith’s other films, mainly the short subjects that he produced while at The Biograph Company, are often lost in comparison, but are potentially just as valuable regarding instructional utilization. There are several areas within National Content Standards that are specifically geared toward older students that are applicable to the study of film

in general. 5 The National Content Standards for history instructors not only drive curriculum subjects, but guide teachers of all ages in the classroom regarding presentation, resources, technology and other materials that are vital to the education of students. Various media forms, including early film could prove vital to the examination of an earlier time, and should be counted as a primary resource to serve as a reflection of the time in which the film was released/produced. Ideally, the films studied will project common dress and behavior as well as common social, political and economic aspects of social history. In short, the extensive filmography of D.W. Griffith would be an ideal teaching tool that will provide insight into an era as well as a multitude of social and political issues that are key when called to define or illustrate the era of the early twentieth century. 

Birth of a Nation is often viewed by historians and film students alike, not only to examine the stereotypical views of the turn of the twentieth century, but for its early film contributions. However, there are several works that bear the Griffith name that are largely ignored. These films should be considered important positive contributions to society, particularly regarding educational tactics. They were produced earlier than Birth of a Nation , and problematically remain unmentioned in their relation to the study of history, by Griffith critics, teachers and historians.

The impact of Birth of a Nation was so great, that not only have Griffith’s other works been overlooked, the director’s reputation in modern times has suffered to such an extent that his technical and artistic contributions to the film world are overshadowed by the now racist image that he carries. Recently, one of Hollywood’s highest honors was renamed due to Griffith’s reputation as a bigot, due to his representations of African Americans in Birth of a Nation . In December of 1999, the board of the Director’s Guild of America chose to rename one of its highest honors, The D.W. Griffith Award, based upon the racial controversy that the director is accused of stimulating. Director’s Guild Award President Jack Shea submitted this response regarding justification for the removal of the award’s name: As we approach a new millennium, the time is right to create a new ultimate honor for film directors that better reflects the sensibilities of our society at this time in our national history… There is no question that D.W. Griffith was a brilliant pioneer filmmaker whose innovations as a visionary film artist led the way for generations of directors. However, it is also true that he helped foster intolerable racial stereotypes.6 D.W. Griffith did write, produce and direct other film works that attempted to spread a positive message regarding race, class and gender prior to 

Birth of a Nation . This thesis will examine the social trends that led to Griffith’s dramatization decisions regarding issues of the early twentieth century, and comparatively analyze them with Griffith’s finished works, interactions with

coworkers, reviews and laws that may have influenced his directorial choices. All of these factors will prove that other films, mainly through the Biograph Film Company are valuable resources that may be utilized for teaching purposes and particularly as primary social and economic documents. An examination will also be made regarding the study of his extensive filmography, and its positive contributions to society and the study of historical and social issues. The bulk of the evidence for such exists within the film products themselves. 

Birth of a Nation created a public stir that centralized upon racial tensions and the question of fairness among races. It also managed to propel the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) to the forefront of public controversy, and ultimately promoted the fight toward racial equality and the recognition of a growing national problem in relation to ethnicity, gender and race. The outcry that the NAACP generated and the negative exposure to 

Birth of a Nation in 1915, aided in Griffith’s recent character demise. Prior to World War II, he was hailed as an artist. Presently, virtually all proof of Griffith’s prowess and knowledge as a filmmaker and business entrepreneur, are generally grouped with the negative criticism that is associated with Birth of a Nation . In all of his films, he created antagonists that paralleled the views of society in general and explored issues that were exploding onto everyday headlines. The problem with the popular theories regarding Griffith’s psyche, is that they are based upon modern day film theory and political views; a far cry from the popular, though perhaps misguided, opinions of the nineteen-teens. He 6

bent the constrictions of gender in his films as well in his professional career, addressed racial issues that were considered taboo and often created sympathetic characters of color on-screen. In analyzing the scope of film, there lies a need for a protagonist and an antagonist. As of 1915, it was common practice to assign the role of villain in dramatic vehicles to those individuals that were considered to be outsiders. These seem to include any deviation from the hard-working white American, or nativist ideal. Examples of specific issues that were a part of Griffith’s notable film shorts include temperance, incest, political corruption and abuse. Racial tension perhaps topped this list as a result of industry-related and occupationally inspired riots after the Reconstruction period incited anti-ethnic attitudes.7 Griffith’s Biograph films reflect all of these issues, and often replicate common public views of the early twentieth century, thus making these fictional dramas, worthy of the title primary resource. Hollywood, even in its infancy, was filled with a bevy of individualized personas, including those whose sexual orientation, racial background and class structure varied. For years, D. W. Griffith was the authority on filmmaking.

Historical Background, Impact, and Griffith Theory Most nativists, or those that considered themselves true Americans, including D.W. Griffith, operated under the theory that the modern United States really did not exist until after the end of the Civil War. Their presumption followed the theory that the origins of the real United States emerged when masses of former slaves were forced to sustain themselves and compete with newly arrived immigrants for jobs, homes and a place within society. “The Public Be Damned: A Thematic and Multiple Intelligence Approach to Teaching the Gilded Age,” describes the tensions that defined the social Darwinist theory at the turn of the twentieth century, as well as outline just what a nativist’s perception of an outsider was. The two authors, Nina Mjagkij and D. Antonio Cantu offer a brief account of some of the social tensions in the U.S. throughout the Gilded Age due to job competition, racial tensions and social mobility issues. While many urban residents migrated to the cities from rural areas in the United States, the majority of the newcomers were immigrants. The concentration of these new arrivals in select urban areas led to the emergence of distinct ethnic neighborhoods and fueled nativist fears. Many native-born white Americans, fearing job competition and race suicide, demanded immigration restriction in an attempt to limit the influx of non-Protestant immigrants.15

Robert Rosenstone also considers written history just as subjective as that of film, thus begging the question of historical legitimacy in general Essentially, he puts dramatic film on an even playing field as that of written history. Second, the narratives that historians write are in fact, “verbal fictions”; written history is a representation of the past, not the past itself. The Life of D.W. Griffith D.W. Griffith’s life was ironically like one of his films. It contained satire, drama and several instances of extreme circumstance. A brief examination of Griffith’s past as well as the era that he existed within, will provide insight regarding his influences, directorial decisions and popular social issues of the time period. All of these pieces contribute to the finished body of film that was produced while at the Biograph Company, and it is from these that educators, historians and students are able to examine valuable political and cultural ideals that were prevalent throughout the early twentieth century. Social Reform Films Recently, academics have made several attempts to defend and justify D.W. Griffith’s questionable judgments both on and off of the camera, again, predominantly in reference to Birth of a Nation . However, the early works of D.W. Griffith, the Biograph short subjects, contain evidence to combat Griffith’s controversial reputation, and often embrace new twentieth century ideals, including social, racial and political concepts that encompass the true melting pot spirit of the U.S. The primary ethnic and racial groups included in the early short films are laborers, women, African Americans, the Chinese, and Native Americans. These individuals encompass the social turbulence within the U.S. in the early twentieth century, generally regarding class and job competition; providing ample material for early silent film subjects that are worthy of present primary resource consideration and study by secondary students in present day classrooms. One of the primary resources utilized to examine D.W. Griffith and his contributions at the Biograph Company include a series of releases called The Biograph Bulletin . A curious aspect of this collection of publications is that there is not an author credited with their composition. However, they clearly bear the Biograph name and thus represent the thoughts, ideas and viewpoint of the 55 

studio. The Biograph Bulletin gives a plot description of each short made by D.W. Griffith, and adds a commentary that may be assessed to the time period; meaning that various verbiage and concepts are written and therefore represented within to allow the reader a further glimpse into the early days of the film company. It further allows the student/reader to speculate as to motivation and other aspects of the creative process and will provide insight regarding Griffith’s directorial decisions and processes. Social Reform Films: Family Issues and Labor Messages D.W. Griffith’s sophistication regarding filmmaking techniques seemed to develop with storylines. Several of his films featured religious ideals of reform, generally those represented within groups such as the Women’s Christian Temperance Union, (WCTU). Ultimately, these subjects often became fuel for Griffith’s storylines. Women were seeking the right to vote, and various political groups were playing for an advantage in recruitment through their promotion of nativist ideals, that included the real American; mainly those that were white, Christian and hard-working. Griffith’s rise to fame paralleled this political and social revolution. Ideals that involved temperance, immigration, labor and industrial practices and leisure activities were being targeted as the root of society’s problems. These issues often conflicted with the old school philosophy of observing the rules that have governed civilized society for over a century. Political groups were often at the heart of a changing and modern America. Theodore Roosevelt was a large champion of fair labor practices and encouraged 56 

individual well-being among workers.88 D.W. Griffith projects these issues through his Biograph shorts. Damon W. Root, a political historian and author of the article, “When Bigots Become Reformers: The Progressive Era’s Shameful Record on Race,” describes the Progressive movement as: The Progressive movement swept America from roughly the early 1890s through the early 1920s, producing a broad popular consensus that government should be the primary agent of social change. To that end, legions of idealistic young crusaders, operating at the local, state, and federal levels, seized and wielded sweeping new powers and enacted a mountain of new legislation, including minimum wage and maximum hour laws, antitrust statutes, restrictions on the sale and consumption of alcohol, appropriations for hundreds of miles or roads and highways, assistance to new immigrants and the poor, women’s suffrage, and electoral reform, among much else.89 The Progressive Era encompassed individuality and capitalism, the very essence of the film industry at its birth. The era exemplified ideals that were largely publicized and spread prior to and surrounding the 1896 election, a time that closely paralleled the film boom. Modernization was a great symbol of the era and concepts including suffrage, immigration, industrial matters utilized media to attract those that were potentially sympathetic to their various platforms.90 Inadvertently, film production, was one of these ways. Gender Among the more forward thinking theories that exist within Griffith’s Biograph short subjects is the concept of the strong woman/female heroine. Often these women carried the film within the compass of an actress, or they were instrumental to the actual production process behind the scenes at Biograph studios. These early works could be perceived as a forward movement for women, and thus would be greatly valued as teaching tools in modern history classrooms. The Biograph shorts are a veritable chronicle of the rise and rebellion of women and their traditional spheres within the home. These early works are largely ignored by instructors and would demonstrate to students the issues that women at that time were facing within their places of business, home and society. At the turn of the twentieth century, women were becoming more and more of a force in the workplace due to financial necessity as well as a desire for independence. As women began to aid in the support of their families through performing tasks traditionally known as “men’s work,” the primary argument for equal rights for both genders festered throughout the United States. The melting pot was near boiling as new faces, races and ideas poured into the urban centers already packed with diverse individuals. Upon the abolition of slavery in the South, women began to express their interest in becoming free of their 70 

husbands’ political theories and practices. They also questioned the various roles that they were destined to play and brought about the question of other occupations rather than that of wife and mother. Eleanor Flexner, a women’s studies scholar and activist summarized: It was in the abolition movement that women first learned to organize, to hold public meetings, to conduct petition campaigns. By: Jaclyn A. Smith Submitted as a fulfillment of the requirements for the Masters of Arts Degree in History The University of Toledo December, 2007 D.W. Griffith capitalized upon already existing theories and social positions in order to present audiences with entertaining plots and dramatic antagonists. Often these subjects consisted of individuals that were potentially marketable regarding public opinion and sensationalism, allowing him to make a name for himself in the film world as a source of artistic and technical innovations. Perhaps known best for his controversial film, Birth of a Nation,1 he has been applauded and crucified by modern historians and analysts regarding his creative practices and basically, spread of racial stereotypes to early film audiences. The denigration of his work by modern scholars lies mainly within the characters and racial tensions that were perpetuated on-screen as a result of his conceptual character options. However, in many of his early films that were produced at the Biograph Company, Griffith initiated exposure for gender, racial and ethnic groups that were largely ignored and propelled these issues to the

forefront of the public eye. Griffith should be celebrated as a filmmaker that used controversy to provoke thought regarding issues of race, class and gender, and certainly his other films have the teaching capability that Birth of a Nation is commonly utilized for. There are several other pieces that were produced by Griffith that are symbolic of public attitudes and accurate representation of society near the turn of the twentieth century. These works should be celebrated as primary resource materials, and therefore used in classrooms to teach political, racial and social issues to students that wish to study such concepts. The evidence for this theory lies not only in his films, but in the behind-the-scenes production occurrences, character references, personal anecdotes and various current and past media sources. Griffith from 1908 to 1919 that have survived through documentation or independently. v

Introduction The utilization of visual aids in a classroom is invaluable as a result of the different learning styles preferred by individual students. Before documentaries and fictional films, students were relied upon still photographs, drawings, maps and words in order to link a visual impression with a body of text. Throughout the twentieth century, film has emerged as an important teaching tool that allows students the experience of actually seeing an occurrence or event either as it happened, or they are able to view a creative representation of the occasion, in regard to fictional depictions. Despite the immense body of work that D.W. Griffith produced between 1908 and 1940, educators usually focus on one controversial film in particular. Birth of a Nation2 is a widely-taught piece in upper-level history courses throughout the U.S. Several reputable institutions, including Virginia Tech’s department of Teaching and Learning use this in various parts of their curriculum to impress upon those that are studying to become teachers the importance of visual aids in instructional situations. At Virginia Tech, Dr. Dave Hicks uses Birth of a Nation to satisfy the National Social Studies Content Standards/expectations and indicates that the film is an apt tool to satisfy the standards that fall under the “Time, Continuity and Change”    

> 2Birth of a Nation, in Griffith Masterworks , DVD, directed by D.W. Griffith (NY: Kino Video, 2002/1915).

Interestingly enough, until the aftermath of World War II, despite the controversy that this film caused, Griffith was applauded for his innovative film techniques, and credited with establishing Birth of a Nation as the first feature-length film. 4 As a result of growing intolerance at the turn of the twentieth century regarding race, gender and ethnicity in the United States, as well as the civil rights movement, recent public and critical opinions regarding Griffith’s character have gone sour. Birth of a Nation , is primarily viewed as an appropriate teaching vehicle for adult or high school education purposes, due to the graphic and emotional scenes that are presented. Sadly, Griffith’s other films, mainly the short subjects that he produced while at The Biograph Company, are often lost in comparison, but are potentially just as valuable regarding instructional utilization. There are several areas within National Content Standards that are specifically geared toward older students that are applicable to the study of film
